| `2026-09-29-lme-full-all`                   | `--expand --aggregate-top-k 40 --chain-of-note` | **92.6%** | **85.0%** | 94.0% | 93.6% |   98.6 | 94.6 | 100.0 |
| `2026-09-30-lme-full-fast`                  | the same, reranker removed                      |     92.6% |     82.0% | 94.0% | 97.4% |  100.0 | 96.4 |  96.7 |
| re-grade of the above by the official judge | gpt-4o, official prompts                        | **92.8%** |     83.5% | 94.0% | 97.4% |   98.6 | 96.4 |  96.6 |

Three readings, and only one of them is a pricing:

1. **88.4 → 92.6 is not a single-variable measurement.** The early full run and the levered one differ in more than
   one thing, so the honest claim is "this route reaches 92.6%", not "the three levers are worth 4.2 points".
2. **The reranker pair is single-variable**, and it is the useful one: same day, same levers, one flag removed —
   MR **85.0 → 82.0**, overall **92.6 → 92.6**. Somebody else, on their own artifact, measured the permutation axis
   at about three MR questions. §13.126.1 computed two from `goldRanks`. Two independent derivations of the same
   small number is the strongest evidence this campaign has that the axis really is priced.
3. **Cross-judge stability**: 92.6% self-judged against 92.8% by the official gpt-4o judge. That is the one thing
   this system has that most of §2.1.2's table does not.

### 13.137.3 The third reading-side axis

| lever                  | what it does                                                                                                                                                                                                                       | does this arm have it                                                       |
| ---------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `--chain-of-note`      | writes per-session date notes inside one call, then computes                                                                                                                                                                       | **yes** — that is `enumerated`                                              |
| `--expand`             | parses time cues (`in April`, `last Thursday`, `from July to October`) and counting/comparison cues (`how many`, `total`, `A and B`, `which came first`) with **rules**, then searches **once per named thing** from a deeper pool | **no**                                                                      |
| `--aggregate-top-k 40` | aggregation questions read 40 candidates instead of the default depth                                                                                                                                                              | **no** — this arm holds top-256 globally, the same depth for every question |

`--expand`'s defining property is that it is **rules, not a model call**. `analyzeQuery` resolves a named period
against `now`, prefers facts whose valid time falls inside it, removes the period from the search words, and issues
one retrieval per named entity. It costs a handful of extra vector searches per question and **no extra LLM call**,
which is why it is affordable at 500 questions and why it is not a prompt experiment at all.

And it is exactly what the campaign's three ceilings do not cover:

- §13.126's ceiling of five questions is a ceiling on **permutations** — every wrong question's gold is already at
  rank 0–18, and no reordering of a list improves its first element.
- §13.133's price of 1.3 questions is the price of **a rule stated in the prompt**, applied by the reader that is
  already getting the question wrong.
- §13.118's budget finding is **withdrawn** by §13.139: 46,622 was a mean, 468 of 500 questions render at or above
  95% of the 48,000 ceiling, and the tightest has 409 characters of room. What that section established and what
  stands is the **pool** result — 95.2% of gold is already in the pool and every wrong question carries its gold.

`--expand` changes **how many separate evidence blocks the reader is handed**, one per named thing. §13.123's
"95.2% of gold is already in the pool" is a statement about the pool's coverage and says nothing about this: the
pool is not enlarged, a different **region** of it is brought in, once per entity, and the blocks arrive side by
side instead of competing for the same top-k slots.

### 13.137.4 Why it lands on exactly the two columns that are short

The levers' two biggest movements are MR **75.9 → 85.0** (+9.1) and TR **85.7 → 94.0** (+8.3), and those are this
arm's two short columns. MR's questions are cross-session counts and comparisons; TR's are date arithmetic. Those
are the two cue classes `analyzeQuery` reads.

There is a counter-consideration that keeps this from being a promise. **This arm's own reference pipeline reaches
MR 106/121 = 87.6% on the control `40751394094` and 105/121 = 86.78% on `40824682542` — with no expansion at all,
only a different instruction block.** So most of the MR gap is closable on the prompt side, and §13.132's `derive`
is testing precisely that. `--expand` is a **second route**, not the only one, and it is not obviously the cheaper
one: `derive` is a line permutation, while `expand` is a retrieval-layer feature with its own tests.

The two runs' reference-arm counts differing by one question is also the third independent sighting of the noise
floor: the same arm on the same dataset, two runs, one question apart.

### 13.137.5 The rule this adds, and how it would have caught the error

**A number in a comparison table must be recomputable from the other side's artifacts, or marked unverified.**
Grading a source is not enough: §6.1 would have given this paper an A for "artifacts published", and the artifacts
are precisely what contradicted the sentence.

Applied here, the check is one table lookup: _does `bench/results/` contain a file whose MR equals 75.9%?_ It does
— `2026-09-29-longmemeval-full` — and that file's own record says which levers were off. The number was right and
the sentence around it was wrong, which is the failure mode a grading rule cannot see.

### 13.137.6 What is registered, and in what order

`derive` is in flight (`40859499624`) against `40751394094`. The ordering after it settles:

- **if MR ≥ 92** (five conversions), most of the gap was the licence's position, `derive` ships, and `expand`
  demotes to a TR candidate — TR is where it has an 8.3-point external movement and MR would have little left;
- **if MR ≤ 90**, `derive` is falsified, `expand` becomes the next registered run, and it is registered against the
  same control so the two are comparable by construction and the ledger's cross-run mode gives the overlap.

Either way the first step is **offline**, because §13.126.4's discipline applies to this axis too: compute, on the
existing 500-question artifact, **how many sub-queries each question decomposes into** and **what each sub-query's
best gold rank is**. If splitting the question does not change which gold turns reach the prompt, the treatment
cannot move accuracy on this dataset and dispatching it would be buying a known zero. That check needs no model
call, which is the point of `--expand` being rules.

## 13.139 "No question reached the ceiling" was read from a mean, and the budget is binding on 468 of 500

### 13.139.1 The reading that has to be withdrawn

§13.118 retired the budget lever with this sentence, repeated in three places:

> the prompt ran at 46,622 characters of a 48,000 budget **with no question at the cap**, so the budget was never
> the constraint and doubling it could only re-arrange.

`46,622` is a **mean**. Read the distribution instead, on the same artifact (`40751394094`):

| statistic                                                |          value |
| -------------------------------------------------------- | -------------: |
| roster median `promptChars`                              |     **46,851** |
| roster p95                                               |         47,394 |
| roster max                                               |     **47,591** |
| questions at or above 95% of the 48,000 ceiling (45,600) | **468 of 500** |
| questions at or above 99% (47,520)                       |              5 |
| questions exactly at 48,000                              |          **0** |

**Ninety-four percent of the roster renders within 2,400 characters of the ceiling, and the largest question is
409 characters short of it.** The budget is not unbound; it is bound on almost every question, and it is bound
_by the renderer_, which is why nothing ever exceeds it.

That is the error, and it is a specific one: **`promptChars` is the length after fitting, so `max < cap` is a
property of the fitting routine and not evidence about the constraint.** The only statistic that answers "is this
lever connected" is how many questions sit near the ceiling, and it was not computed.

### 13.139.2 What survives from §13.118, and it is the part that mattered

The section's other two findings are untouched, and separating them is what makes the correction useful rather
than merely embarrassing:

- **§13.123's coverage census stands**: 95.2% of gold units are in the pool, and **every** one of the 83 wrong
  questions has its gold inside the prompt. So "raise the pool" still buys nothing — not because the budget is
  loose, but because there is no unreached gold to buy.
- **The permutation ceiling stands**: §13.126.1's five questions come from `goldRanks`, which is independent of
  the budget entirely.

What falls is only the third: "doubling the budget could only re-arrange". Doubling it would in fact admit
roughly **twice as many turns** on 468 questions — it would just not admit any more **gold**, which is a different
sentence with a different consequence. The wrong version closed an axis on the grounds that the lever was not
attached; the right version closes it on the grounds that the lever is attached to a reservoir that is empty of
what the arm needs.

### 13.139.3 The distinction §13.118 conflated: pool depth and render width

| quantity                              | value on `40751394094` | what it constrains                    |
| ------------------------------------- | ---------------------: | ------------------------------------- |
| `relevanceTopK`                       |          **256** turns | how many candidates retrieval returns |
| `evidenceTurns` on a typical question |                **166** | how many of them are rendered         |
| `maxTurnChars`                        |                    400 | how long one rendered turn may be     |
| `promptChars`                         |          46,851 median | what the reader actually sees         |

Retrieval returns 256 and the prompt shows 166, so **the pool is not the constraint and never was** — §13.118 was
right about that, and it was right for the pool. But it then used the pool's conclusion to retire the **character
budget**, and those are two different reservoirs. The character budget is where 90 spare turns go to die.

### 13.139.4 What this does to the decomposition axis, measured before it was dispatched

§13.138.4's claim 5 said a decomposition would have to fit its extra turns inside the budget, and that this could
be tested without dispatching anything. Tested:

| quantity, over the 42 cued-and-wrong MR/TR questions |                                value |
| ---------------------------------------------------- | -----------------------------------: |
| median `promptChars`                                 |                               46,305 |
| max `promptChars`                                    |                               47,265 |
| **headroom on the tightest question**                | **735 characters — under two turns** |
| questions at or above 95% of the ceiling             |                         **42 of 42** |

**The prediction is already falsified.** A treatment that adds evidence for one question at a time cannot place
it: there is room for fewer than two additional turns on every single question it would target. So `expand` in the
form `al-buddy-memory` implements it — one retrieval per named thing, added to what is already there — is **not
available to this arm at this budget**, and that is known before writing a line of it.

It is still available in the form this arm's own discipline already prescribes: **§8's fourth rule, that a budget
re-spends evidence rather than appending after it.** `reviewPass` does exactly that with `fitToBudget`, selecting
again instead of adding. A decomposition would have to do the same — replace the 166 turns with "the best turns
for entity A, then for entity B, then for entity C", spending the same 46,851 characters — and that is a different
treatment with a different risk profile: it can lose evidence that the single query had.

### 13.139.5 The rule this adds

**A constraint is measured by how close the results sit to it, not by whether they exceed it.** For any quantity
produced by a fitting routine — `promptChars`, a fitted k, a truncated list — "the maximum is below the cap" is a
statement about the routine. The question is the distribution's mass near the cap, and this campaign now has a
number for the one constraint it cares most about: **468 of 500 questions at or above 95%.**

Applied forward: `acceptance.ts` and every future ceiling check report the **mass near the limit**, not the max.
The prior reading was not a careless sentence — 46,622 was a real mean on a real artifact — it was the wrong
statistic for the question, and the wrong statistic pointed away from a live lever.

## 13.140 Every artifact in this campaign was silent about its own bill, and the reason is one dropped field

### 13.140.1 The omission

Every provider on the OpenAI-compatible wire returns a `usage` block on every response. `complete()` in
`cortex-ai/src/llm/openai-compatible.ts` read the body for `choices` and returned `choices[0].message.content`,
and the block was discarded at that one line.

The consequence is not that the campaign was expensive. It is that **no artifact in this campaign could state
what a run cost**, so no experiment could ask whether a change made one. Every reading in §13.1–§13.139 that
lengthened a prompt — a two-step contract, an enumeration, a licence moved six lines — was registered on
accuracy alone, and the price of each was a fact about an invoice arriving days later. Two of the eleven
registered asks were abandoned for destroying accuracy; none was ever priced.

This is the fifth instance of the shape this repository keeps finding, and the first one outside the measurement
code: a value produced on every request, carried through the transport, and dropped at the one hop where it
would have been compared. `tools/ledger.mjs --across` is the same failure on the answer side (§13.135), and
`usage` was in the response body the whole time.

### 13.140.2 What the instrument is

`cortex-ai/src/usage.ts`: a parser, one process-wide ledger, and a reading.

| name          | what it does                                                          | why it is where it is                                                 |
| ------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `parseUsage`  | reads `prompt_tokens`, `completion_tokens`, `prompt_cache_hit_tokens` | the only place that decides what a usable block is                    |
| `recordUsage` | one call, priced or unpriced                                          | called from `complete()`, the one hop every request passes through    |
| `llmUsage`    | a snapshot of the ledger                                              | process-wide, because the ten call sites cannot thread a counter down |
| `usageDelta`  | one run's spend, from two snapshots                                   | so a library function never has to know where a run begins            |

Two readings the ledger refuses to conflate, and both are the point:

**Absent is not zero.** A response with no `usage` block is an unpriced call, and it is counted as a call. Ten
call sites reporting a `0` token total for a run that spent twelve million is the artifact saying "free" about
a bill, and that is strictly worse than saying nothing.

**A cache hit is a subset of the prompt, not an addition to it.** `prompt_cache_hit_tokens` is the part of
`prompt_tokens` the provider served from its prefix cache. Summing the two would report a bill up to twice the
real one; the ledger adds the hit to its own column and never to `promptTokens`, and a hit larger than the
prompt is dropped to `0` rather than believed — the run then understates its own discount, which is the safe
direction for a number that will be used to decide whether reordering a 47,000-character prompt is worth a run.

### 13.140.3 What it does not measure

- **The embedder.** Zhipu is a different adapter on a different wire and its spend is not in this ledger. An
  embedding cache hit rate is a separate instrument (§13.97 measures the cache, not the tokens).
- **Requests that never produced a response.** A retry that fails on six attempts issues six prompts and leaves
  no usage block. `retryStats().attempts` counts them; `llmUsage().calls` does not. **So `llmUsage` is a lower
  bound on the bill, by construction**, and the gap is exactly the traffic that failed.
- **Whether a timed-out generation was billed.** It may have been. This is why the number is stated as a lower
  bound and not as a reconciliation.

What it does measure, indirectly and usefully: **the retry multiplier.** A run over 500 questions and two sides
issues exactly 1,000 answer calls plus a judge call per answer, so `calls` above that baseline is traffic that was
re-sent -- and every one of those carries its own `promptTokens`. A question that timed out once and succeeded on
the second attempt therefore appears as two priced calls, which is the number §13.140.6 needs before it can cut
anything: the excess is not invisible here, it is priced.

### 13.140.4 Acceptance criteria, and how each was tested

| #   | criterion                                               | test                                                                                                                        |
| --- | ------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 1   | a missing block yields `undefined`, never zeros         | `usage.test.ts` — `parseUsage(undefined)`/`(null)`                                                                          |
| 2   | a block missing either count is rejected whole          | `parseUsage({prompt_tokens: 10})`                                                                                           |
| 3   | a non-integer, negative or non-finite count is rejected | four cases, `Number.NaN` and `∞` included                                                                                   |
| 4   | a cache hit above the prompt is dropped, not believed   | `{prompt: 100, hit: 500}` → `hit: 0`                                                                                        |
| 5   | **the adapter actually calls the parser**               | `llm.test.ts` against a real HTTP server: `complete()` on a body carrying `usage` moves the ledger by exactly those numbers |
| 6   | a response without a block is one call, zero priced     | same server, other shape: `calls: 1, unpricedCalls: 1`                                                                      |
| 7   | a run with no instrumented call omits the field         | `attachLlmUsage` returns its argument **by identity**                                                                       |
| 8   | an all-unpriced run still attaches                      | `calls: 1000, unpricedCalls: 1000` survives                                                                                 |
| 9   | the section survives persistence                        | rendered from a JSON round-trip of the report                                                                               |
| 10  | the two warnings partition                              | all-unpriced → `NO PROVIDER COST WAS REPORTED`; partial → `PARTIAL`; neither fires when all priced                          |
| 11  | the section is a footnote, not a banner                 | index of `Δ accuracy` < index of `Provider spend`                                                                           |

Criterion 5 is the one that matters and the one that cannot be tested at the parse layer. A parser with perfect
tests and no caller is precisely what the campaign had before this section: the number was available on every
request and nothing read it. Mutating the single line `recordUsage(parseUsage(json.usage))` out of `complete()`
fails criteria 5 and 6 and nothing else — which is the evidence that the transport tests reach the transport.

Coverage, per dimension, on the packages touched: `cortex-ai` **100 / 100 / 100 / 100** (with `usage.ts` at
100 on all four); `cortex-eval` **99.59 / 99.08 / 99.80 / 99.59** over 2,415 tests. The census reports one new
orphan, `cortex-ai: LlmUsage`, recorded in `tools/export-census-baseline.json` with the reason: it is the shape
two signatures use and no call site names it, so `export` is required by the declaration and unearned by the
call graph.

### 13.140.5 The three questions this makes answerable, registered with predictions

The first artifact produced after this section is the first one whose spend can be read. Three predictions go
on record now so that the reading is a test and not a description:

| #   | prediction                                                       | falsified by                                                                                       |
| --- | ---------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 1   | `promptTokens` for one memory-arm run is between **10M and 14M** | outside that band, which would mean the prompt is not what `promptChars` says it is                |
| 2   | the prefix-cache share of the prompt is **under 5%**             | a share ≥ 20%, which would make prompt ORDER a live cost lever                                     |
| 3   | `unpricedCalls` is **0** against DeepSeek                        | any non-zero value, which would mean a proxy strips the block or the instrument is not in the path |

Prediction 2 is the one with a decision attached. The prompt is question-specific from its first evidence line,
so the only reusable prefix is the fixed instruction block — a few hundred tokens of 47,000 characters. If the
share comes back at 3%, prompt ordering is settled: there is nothing to win by moving a stable block to the
front. If it comes back near 20%, the instruction block is far larger than its character count suggests (the
six route-specific contracts are candidates), and reordering becomes a registered experiment with a measurable
prize. **The measurement decides which; no reading of the source can.**

**Amended before the first reading, not after it.** §13.147.3 decomposes this prediction, because the dispatch
that answers it runs four repetitions and passes 2-4 send byte-identical requests: the share the artifact
reports is dominated by repetition reuse rather than by prompt ordering, and prediction 1's 10-14M band is
compatible with both a cold single pass and a warm four-pass dispatch. Prediction 2's threshold is retained;
what §13.147.3 adds is which of three readings a given share licenses, and prediction 4 -- the share lands in
the 60-80% band -- registered there while the artifact was still in flight.

### 13.140.6 What this does not licence

Three ways to cut the bill exist and none of them is taken here, for three different reasons:

**Cutting the control arm.** Every dispatch re-derives the same 500 control answers at full price. Caching them
would nearly halve the cost and would destroy the noise floor: the 7.08% flip rate on untouched questions
(§13.135) is _the control re-deriving itself_, and a cached control would make every future treatment look
significant. The control's re-derivation is the cheapest measurement in the campaign.

**Cutting `runs`.** Repetitions are what separate a +1.5-point artifact from a 1.4σ fluctuation. Buying the
same reading with fewer samples is buying a smaller experiment, not a cheaper one.

**Cutting the prompt.** The window is the independent variable of this entire arm. §13.139 established that 468
of 500 questions sit at 95% of the ceiling; shrinking it is a treatment, and one that has already been
measured in the other direction (§13.16).

What remains is the traffic that buys nothing, and it needs one more counter before it can be cut: **a timed-out
attempt re-sends the full prompt**, up to `maxRetries` times, and a generation that times out after 300 s on a
12,000-token prompt pays for that prompt again. The registered threshold is one number — if any artifact of a
future run reports a retry exhaustion with `attempts > 1` on a deadline, the next dispatch caps **timeout**
retries at 1, because a deadline that has fired twice is not a transient network fault. Transient 5xx and reset
retries keep their budget: those are the case the ladder exists for.

### 13.140.7 The rule this adds

**An artifact that cannot state its own bill cannot be compared on cost, and a cost claim made before the
instrument existed is a claim about an invoice.** Applied forward: every registered treatment from here carries
its `llmUsage` beside its accuracy delta, and a treatment that buys one question for 40% more prompt is now a
trade a reader can price rather than a sentence about token efficiency.

## 13.141 `review_pass=recover` was two mechanisms behind one field, and one of them was a withdrawal

### 13.141.1 What the field actually named

`review_pass` accepts four names — `none`, `audit`, `recover`, `bare` — and the arm derived a second
option from it:

```ts
reviewBareDecline: readReviewPass(env[REVIEW_PASS_VARIABLE]) === 'bare',
```

That equality is wrong, and its wrongness is a property of the **route table**, not of the string.
The two passes act on populations that do not overlap:

| pass          | where it is wired      | what it fires on                                                 | routes                                                                                              |
| ------------- | ---------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| bare ladder   | `#answerWithBareRetry` | a first-pass reply that is the abstention token and nothing else | `flat`, `temporal`, `assistant`, `knowledge-update` — **not** `abstention`, **not** `multi-session` |
| recovery pass | `#promptSessionAware`  | a decline whose own Step 1 list is non-empty                     | `multi-session` only                                                                                |

So `review_pass=recover` **removed** the bare ladder from four routes while adding the recovery pass to
one. §13.128 registers that dispatch as a single-field experiment whose pass "can only ever consult on
questions that are already wrong"; under the coupled reading that sentence is false twice — the run
would also have measured the withdrawal of a shipped treatment, and any question the bare ladder had
converted would have gone back to being a decline. Nothing in the artifact would have shown it: one
field changes, and the loss arrives inside the accuracy delta.

This is the §13.129.1 shape one layer up. There the assembly check found `askRoutes` had silently
narrowed to `flat`; here the _derivation_ narrows a second option. Both are a dispatch that does not
administer the experiment its registration names.

**The control's own censuses size the withdrawal**, and the number is not small:

| field       | control `40751394094` (`review_pass=bare`) | meaning                                                                                          |
| ----------- | ------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `bareRetry` | `{attempted: 92, answered: 92}`            | the ladder re-asked **92 times across 4 runs** — 23 per run — and every retry returned an answer |
| `recovery`  | `{attempted: 0, answered: 0}`              | the recovery pass never fired, because it was never on                                           |

A decline is wrong on every capability whose gold is not a decline, so those 92 re-asks were 92 places
where a null could become a correct answer. §13.128's own premise — "the pass can only ever consult on
questions that are already wrong" — is true of the recovery pass and was about to be false of the run:
the dispatch would have withdrawn 92 consultations to gain at most 10, and the artifact would have shown
one field changing. That is a factor of nine in the wrong direction, invisible in the configuration line.

### 13.141.2 The reach was also overstated, and for the same reason

§13.128.1 counted declines that carry a Step 1 list across all six capabilities and concluded **16
reachable (10 MR, 5 TR, 1 KU)**. The recovery pass is inside the multi-session path, and `MR` is the
only capability routed there (`evidenceRouteOf`). `TR` goes to `answerTemporal`, `KU` to
`answerKnowledgeUpdate`, `ABS` to `answerAbstention`, everything else to `answer`.

| capability    | declines | with a list | route              | reached by `recover` |
| ------------- | -------: | ----------: | ------------------ | -------------------- |
| MR            |       12 |      **10** | `multi-session`    | **10**               |
| TR            |        8 |           5 | `temporal`         | 0                    |
| KU            |        2 |           1 | `knowledge-update` | 0                    |
| ABS           |       29 |           0 | `abstention`       | 0 — structurally     |
| IE            |        1 |           0 | `flat`             | 0                    |
| **reachable** |       52 |          16 |                    | **10**               |

Ten questions, not sixteen: the ceiling is **2.0 points**, not 3.2. The six that the earlier count
included were never in the treated population, which is the same error §13.132.1 records for a
criterion computed on the wrong denominator — this time the denominator was a capability census when
the mechanism is wired by route.

### 13.141.3 The repair, at the layer where the field lives

`carriesBareLadder(pass)` in `bench-memory-arm.ts`:

```ts
function carriesBareLadder(pass: string): boolean {
  return pass === 'bare' || pass === 'recover';
}
```

The repair is in the arm and **not** in `CortexMemory`, and that placement is the decision. The
product keeps `reviewPass` and `reviewBareDecline` orthogonal: both, either, or neither are all
expressible, and a product-level coupling would delete a configuration the type offers. What has one
field is the **dispatch**, so the dispatch is what names a configuration — and the artifact already
records both facts separately (`memoryArmConfig.reviewPass` and `memoryArmConfig.reviewBareDecline`),
so a reader can still see which mechanism was on without reconstructing it from a coupling.

`audit` stays out. It re-asks with the whole window, so a bare retry under it would make any movement
two consultations rather than one — the same reason `CortexMemory`'s constructor refuses `audit`
beside a vote.

One more fact worth stating, because it makes the attribution sharper than the arm-level view
suggests: `bare` is **not** a member of the product's `ReviewPass` (`'none' | 'audit' | 'recover'`).
`run-ablation.ts` maps `bare` to "no review pass" plus `reviewBareDecline: true`, and `recover` now
maps to `reviewPass: 'recover'` plus the same `reviewBareDecline: true`. So the product-level
difference between the control and the treatment is **exactly one field** — `reviewPass`, absent
against `'recover'` — and the bare ladder is identical on both sides rather than merely present on
both sides. That is the shape the registration asked for; the equality in §13.141.1 was preventing
it.

### 13.141.4 Acceptance criteria, and how each was tested

| #   | criterion                                                     | test                                                                                   |
| --- | ------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 1   | `bare` still means what it meant                              | `review-pass-ladder.test.ts` — `reviewPass: 'bare'`, `reviewBareDecline: true`         |
| 2   | `recover` carries the bare ladder as well                     | same file — `recover` ⇒ both true                                                      |
| 3   | `audit` and `none` carry neither                              | same file, both names                                                                  |
| 4   | the two names stay distinguishable in the artifact            | `reviewPass` differs, `reviewBareDecline` equal                                        |
| 5   | a flat bare decline is re-asked under the union               | `review-ladder.test.ts` — 2 calls, `bareRetry {1,1}`, `recovery {0,0}`                 |
| 6   | a listed multi-session decline is re-asked under the union    | same — 2 calls, `recovery {1,1}`, `bareRetry {0,0}`                                    |
| 7   | **one consultation per decline on either route**              | same — two declines, two routes, exactly 4 calls                                       |
| 8   | `review_pass=bare` leaves MR unrecovered                      | same — 1 call, `recovery {0,0}`: the archived state, which §13.128 assumed was covered |
| 9   | `recover` without the ladder leaves a flat decline unanswered | same — 1 call: exactly what the old derivation produced                                |

Criterion 7 is the one that matters for attribution: disjointness is asserted by counting calls across
two routes in one instance, not by reading the call graph. Criterion 9 is the regression this file
exists to prevent, kept as a live test rather than a paragraph.

Mutation: restoring `=== 'bare'` fails criteria 2 and 4 and nothing else.

### 13.141.5 The predictions, restated on the population the mechanism can reach

§13.128.3's four claims are kept, with the numbers their own populations imply:

| #     | claim                                                                                                      | falsified by                                                                                    |
| ----- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **1** | at least **4 of the 10** reachable MR questions convert to correct                                         | fewer than 4 — the old "5 of 16" was a floor set on a population six of which cannot be reached |
| **2** | **ABS does not move** (29/30 question for question)                                                        | any ABS verdict change — the abstention route is excluded in both passes                        |
| **3** | no `flat`/`temporal`/`assistant`/`knowledge-update` question that declined bare changes verdict            | a flip there: the ladder is carried, so a flip means the union did not reach the option         |
| **4** | the counting questions among the 10 are likelier to convert, because the corrective prompt names the count | zero of them convert while non-counting ones do                                                 |

Claim 1 drops from 5 to 4 with the population, and it is worth saying why the ratio barely moves: the
six removed are the TR and KU declines, which this pass never reaches, so the _rate_ the earlier
registration implied (5/16 = 31%) is preserved at 4/10 = 40% only because the removed questions were
the ones least likely to convert — a flat-context decline whose list exists but whose answer needs a
window the corrective prompt does not re-send.

### 13.141.6 The rule this adds

**A treatment's reach is a property of the route table, and a dispatch field that names a
configuration must be derived by a tested function rather than by string equality.** Applied forward:
every registered treatment from here states the route it is wired into beside the population it
counts, and every env-var-to-option derivation that is not an identity gets a test that names the
configuration the name covers.

## 13.142 The prompt's invariant prefix is ten characters, so the cache prediction was a consequence and not a measurement

### 13.142.1 What the renderer actually puts first

`buildPrompt` assembles one string:

```
EVIDENCE:
<turns, question-specific from the first byte>

QUESTION: <question>

<instruction block>
```

The instruction — the only text identical on every question a route answers — is **last**. `tools/prompt-anatomy.mjs`
renders each `(contract, ask)` cell with no evidence and an empty question and reports the instruction's size
against the roster's measured median prompt (46,851 characters, §13.139):

| contract                     | instruction characters | share of a 46,851-char prompt |
| ---------------------------- | ---------------------: | ----------------------------: |
| `extractive`                 |                    393 |                         0.84% |
| `abstention`                 |                    315 |                         0.67% |
| `temporal`                   |                    571 |                         1.22% |
| `assistant`                  |                    341 |                         0.73% |
| `knowledge-update`           |                    512 |                         1.09% |
| `abstention-evidence-blocks` |                    315 |                         0.67% |

So the anatomy of one prompt is: **~1% instruction, ~99% evidence and the question line.**

### 13.142.2 Prediction 2 of §13.140.5, settled without a run

That section registered three predictions and left the middle one to the first instrumented artifact:

> 2. the prefix-cache share of the prompt is **under 5%** — falsified by a share ≥ 20%, which would make prompt
>    ORDER a live cost lever

A prefix cache matches a **prefix**. The prefix here is `EVIDENCE:\n` and it stops being question-independent
immediately after — **ten characters, 0.02%** of the prompt. The share cannot be 20% for any provider, because
there is nothing before the evidence to match. The prediction is not a measurement waiting for a bill; it is a
consequence of the layout, and the tool now computes it with no model call.

The decision attached to it is therefore also settled, and in the direction the section said it would go:

| order                    | invariant prefix | share of the prompt | verdict                                          |
| ------------------------ | ---------------: | ------------------: | ------------------------------------------------ |
| evidence first (shipped) |         10 chars |               0.02% | —                                                |
| instruction first        |      ≤ 571 chars |             ≤ 1.22% | the **entire** prize a reordering could ever win |

**Reordering the prompt to make its instruction block cacheable is worth at most 1.2% of the bill**, before
accounting for its accuracy risk (the instruction is last because the reader reads it after the evidence, and
`fitToBudget` shrinks evidence to keep it intact, §12.9). That is not worth a dispatch, and the tool is what makes
that a priced decision rather than an intuition.

### 13.142.3 What the bill actually is, which is the answer to "where can tokens be cut"

The five cost levers this campaign could reach, priced by this measurement:

| lever                                                   | size                                                   | status                                                              |
| ------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| instruction length / prompt engineering                 | **0.67–1.22%** of the bill                             | not a lever: a 50% shorter instruction saves 0.4%                   |
| prefix-cache reuse via reordering                       | ≤ 1.22%                                                | not a lever (§13.142.2)                                             |
| evidence volume per question                            | **~99%**                                               | the only lever with a prize                                         |
| turns per question (window policy)                      | scales the 99% linearly                                | the arm's independent variable (§13.139: 468/500 at 95% of the cap) |
| assistant-turn share of the rendered room               | **51.9%** (§13.82)                                     | the largest addressable slice inside the 99%                        |
| retry traffic (a timed-out attempt re-sends the prompt) | priced by `llmUsage.calls` above 1,000/run (§13.140.4) | registered, threshold set                                           |

The conclusion is uncomfortable and therefore worth stating plainly: **this campaign cannot buy accuracy with
cheaper prompts.** Every ask registered in §13.1–§13.141 that lengthened the instruction lengthened the bill by
under 1%, and every ask that shortened it saved under 1%. The cost of this arm is the evidence it renders, which
is also the thing whose size is being varied on purpose (§13.16, §13.82, §13.139).

### 13.142.4 Acceptance criteria, and how each was tested

| #   | criterion                                                                    | test                                                                          |
| --- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 1   | every contract × ask cell renders a non-empty instruction                    | `test_prompt_anatomy.py` — 66 cells                                           |
| 2   | the prompt begins with `EVIDENCE:\n`, and the tool refuses one that does not | the tool throws; the count is asserted as `len('EVIDENCE:\n')` for every cell |
| 3   | the instruction is under 2% of a real prompt                                 | every cell, against 46,851                                                    |
| 4   | reordering's ceiling is the instruction block, not the prompt                | `prefixIfReordered == instruction` and `> prefixToday`                        |
| 5   | the report names the ask under test and prints the whole grid                | `--ask derive --contract temporal`                                            |
| 6   | an unrecognised argument is refused rather than ignored                      | `--nonsense` exits non-zero                                                   |

Criterion 2 is the one that keeps the tool honest: its headline claim is a property of the **order**, so the tool
asserts the order and fails loudly rather than reporting a number that a future reordering would silently invert.
Mutation: `prefixToday: 0` fails criterion 2 and nothing else.

### 13.142.5 The rule this adds

**A prediction that is computable from the source is not a measurement, and spending a run to confirm one is
spending a run on an arithmetic exercise.** Applied forward: every registered prediction is now checked against
`tools/` before it is dispatched — if a tool can compute it, the tool computes it and the registration records the
computation, so the dispatch is spent only on what needs a model.

## 13.143 `derive` reproduced its mechanism to the character and lost six questions: MR's verdicts are order-sensitive at 15%

### 13.143.1 The assembly check, before any accuracy is read

Run **`40859499624`**, `ask=derive`, control **`40751394094`** (`ask=enumerated`, `reviewPass=bare`, `T=0`).

| criterion                          | reading                                                           | verdict                     |
| ---------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------- |
| `ask`                              | `enumerated` → `derive`                                           | intended                    |
| `askRoutes`                        | unchanged on the arm's three routes                               | intended                    |
| **`promptChars`, all 500 records** | **MR 121/121, TR 127/127, IE 150/150, KU 72/72, ABS 30/30 equal** | **the permutation is real** |

That last row is §13.132.5's prediction 1 and it is the strongest mechanism reading in this document: the treatment
is a **row permutation** of two blocks, so every prompt must keep its length to the character, and 500 of 500 did.
No other treatment in §13.1–§13.142 could assert this — the others regenerate text and can only assert that the
prompt _changed_.

So the sentence moved, on every question, and nothing else did. What follows is a reading of what moving it cost.

### 13.143.2 The result, and the comparison that had to be redone

The first read of this run compared **first repetitions** — the practice every earlier section in this document
follows — and reported MR 87 → 81. The artifact also carries the **four-run distribution per capability**, and
reading it changes what the difference is:

| capability  |       n | control rep 1 | derive rep 1 | control mean (min–max) | derive mean (min–max)  |      Δ mean |
| ----------- | ------: | ------------: | -----------: | ---------------------- | ---------------------- | ----------: |
| IE          |     150 |           140 |          142 | 140.25 (139–142)       | 142.50 (141–145)       |        +2.3 |
| **MR**      | **121** |        **87** |       **81** | **86.50 (83–89)**      | **83.00 (81–87)**      |    **−3.5** |
| TR          |     127 |           100 |          105 | 102.50 (100–105)       | 103.25 (101–105)       |        +0.8 |
| KU          |      72 |            61 |           62 | 62.75 (61–64)          | 63.00 (62–64)          |        +0.3 |
| ABS         |      30 |            29 |           29 | 29.00 (29–29)          | 29.00 (29–29)          |           0 |
| **overall** |     500 |        83.40% |       83.80% | **84.20%** (83.4–84.8) | **84.15%** (83.8–85.0) | **−0.05pp** |

Three facts follow, and the first one is about the instrument rather than the treatment:

1. **Four repetitions of ONE configuration span six questions on MR** — the control alone ranges 83–89. The
   difference this run produced is −3.5 on the mean, and **the derive distribution's top (87) is inside the
   control's range (83–89)**. The two configurations are not distinguishable on MR by this design.
2. **The overall means differ by 0.05 points** (84.20% against 84.15%, i.e. a quarter of a question), while the
   first-repetition pair read +2. The +2 was the noisiest available comparison and it is not the run's result.
3. **Every registered threshold still fails**, because the thresholds were set on first-repetition numbers: MR
   declines 12 → 11 (≤7 wanted), 3 of the 10 winnable converted (≥5 wanted), MR 83.0/121 = 68.6% on the mean
   (< 76.0% wanted), overall mean 84.15% (< 84.2 wanted). A refutation does not need a sign test — but the _reason_
   for it is "no movement at this resolution", not "six questions lost".

### 13.143.3 The attribution, which the instrument could not compute until it was repaired

`ledger.mjs --across` splits treated from untouched by `promptChars`, and this treatment **has no prompt-length
change by construction** — it printed `0 treated questions` and an attribution failure about a run that had
reached 121. The tool now takes the population from the mechanism (`--treated capability=MR`):

```
    split by capability in {MR}
  treated   : 121 questions, bought 6, sold 12, net -6
  untouched : 379 questions, bought 18, sold 10, net +8
    ... the treatment's excess is -8.6 question(s)
    flip rate: treated 14.9% (18/121), untouched 7.4% (28/379)
    NO GAIN ...
    and the excess is NEGATIVE: ... a regression and not a null
```

That reading is correct **for the first repetition**, which is what the tool pairs on, and it is the reading that
made the means worth computing: −8.6 questions of excess on one draw, against a within-configuration range of six
questions on MR alone. The tool's own docblock says a paired delta is a pairing of draws; this run is the case that
makes that limit visible, and §13.144 records the repair.

### 13.143.4 What this run actually measured, which is bigger than the sentence it was about

The sentence is dead — not because it lost six questions, but because **it moved nothing that this design can
resolve**: MR −3.5 of 121 on the mean with the two ranges overlapping, and the overall mean flat to a quarter of a
question. What survives is a measurement about the **instrument**, and it is worth more than the sentence:

**A row permutation flips 18 of 121 MR verdicts (14.9%) between two runs whose prompts differ in no other way.**
The untouched capabilities, which read byte-identical prompts, flip 28 of 379 (7.4%) — the rate §13.135 measured
at 33 of 466 (7.08%). So the permutation **doubled the per-draw instability** on the one capability it touched,
without moving the mean.

Four consequences:

1. **Per-draw flip rate is not the resolution of a reported mean.** 18 flips on 121 questions gives a per-draw net
   with a standard deviation of about four questions; averaged over the four repetitions the report already
   carries, the resolution of the **mean** is about ±3 questions. Conflating the two — which this section did in
   its first draft, before the distributions were read — overstates the noise by a factor of three and would have
   declared a null a regression.
2. **First-repetition comparisons are the noisiest comparison available, and this campaign has been making them.**
   §13.129.1, §13.132.5 and §13.133 all quote first-repetition numbers because `questions[]` carries one draw per
   question. The per-capability means were in the same artifact the whole time.
3. **MR is order-sensitive at 14.9% per draw**, which is the strongest statement this run supports and is three
   times the reader's byte-identical instability. Any MR treatment whose effect is a few questions still needs the
   mean, and any MR treatment that is a _reordering_ needs the mean plus a reason to believe order does not simply
   add variance.
4. **§13.133's prompt-axis pricing is priced per draw, not per mean.** Its +1.3 questions is below the per-draw
   resolution and near the mean's; it stands for the routes it measured and remains unread on MR.

### 13.143.5 What this does not license

**It does not license "the licence sentence is fine where it was."** The move did not help, and the position it
moved _from_ is still the position that leaves MR at 86.5 of 121, with §13.56's rule — a reader that lists items
and then declines — still the largest single block of that loss. What died is _this_ edit, not the diagnosis.

**It does not license a second permutation attempt.** Any further rearrangement lives in the same ±10 band, so it
would need either a much larger population or a different route to the same evidence. The registered replacement is
`recover` (§13.128 / §13.141), which is one-sided by construction and does not depend on this band at all.

### 13.143.6 The rule this adds

**A mechanism that reproduces to the character can still be unmeasurable at the population it acts on, so the flip
rate of the treated bucket is read before the net is compared with anything.** Applied forward: every registration
whose mechanism is a reordering, a rename or a single-sentence move states the flip rate it expects on its treated
population, and a threshold below that rate is refused at registration rather than reported as a null afterwards.

## 13.144 The artifact carried four repetitions and this campaign kept quoting the first one

### 13.144.1 The defect, and the run that exposed it

`questions[]` holds **one record per question**: the first repetition. Every paired delta in this document is
computed from it — `ledger.mjs --across`, `discordantQuestions`, §13.129.1's assembly checks, §13.132.5's
thresholds, §13.133's pricing. All of them compare **one draw against one draw**.

The same artifact carries `ablation.featureAggregate` and `ablation.featureByCapability`, each `{min, avg, max}`
over the four repetitions it paid for. Nothing in `tools/` read them.

Run `40859499624` is where the two readings diverge by enough to change a verdict:

| reading                  | MR                       | overall                       |
| ------------------------ | ------------------------ | ----------------------------- |
| first repetition, paired | 87 → 81 (**−6**)         | 83.40% → 83.80% (**+2**)      |
| mean over four runs      | 86.50 → 83.00 (**−3.5**) | 84.20% → 84.15% (**−0.05pp**) |

and the distributions behind the means:

|         | control   | derive    |
| ------- | --------- | --------- |
| MR      | 83–89     | 81–87     |
| overall | 83.4–84.8 | 83.8–85.0 |

**Four repetitions of one configuration span six questions on MR.** The difference the run produced is inside a
single configuration's own range, and the derive distribution's top (87) is inside the control's (83–89). Reported
from first repetitions, that is "MR lost six questions"; reported from the means, it is "no movement this design
can resolve". Both sentences are arithmetic over the same file.

### 13.144.2 What the tool does now

`--across` reads both distributions and prints them **after the split**, because the split says _which_ questions
moved and this says whether the amount is larger than the run's own repetitions:

```
      per-capability means over all repetitions, which is the comparison the delta above is not:
        MR: control 86.50 (83-89), derive 83.00 (81-87) -- ranges OVERLAP
        ...
      overall mean: control 84.20% (83.4-84.8), derive 84.15% (83.8-85.0), delta -0.05 points
```

Two rules it encodes, both narrow:

**A negative excess changes its sentence when the ranges overlap.** Without the distributions, a negative excess
is the only signal available and it is worth stating as a regression — that is what §13.143.3's first reading said.
With them, and with the ranges overlapping, the same arithmetic is a draw-to-draw fluctuation:

```
      the excess is negative on THIS PAIR OF DRAWS, but the two runs' repetition ranges
      overlap (below), so it is not a separation
```

**A report without a distribution says so.** "`this report carries no per-run distribution, so the delta above is
one draw against one draw`" is the honest caption for every artifact produced before this section, and it costs one
line.

The overlap test is a range comparison and nothing more: it says whether two four-point samples could have come
from one configuration, not whether a difference is significant. A p-value over four repetitions would be a claim
this artifact cannot support, and §13.135.6's rule about pricing with the wrong denominator applies to it.

### 13.144.3 Acceptance criteria, and how each was tested

| #   | criterion                                                     | test                                                                                          |
| --- | ------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 1   | the means are printed beside the paired delta, per capability | `test_ledger.py` — `test_the_reading_prints_the_per_capability_means_beside_the_paired_delta` |
| 2   | overlapping overall ranges take the regression wording back   | `test_overlapping_ranges_take_the_regression_wording_back`                                    |
| 3   | separated ranges keep it                                      | `test_separated_ranges_keep_the_regression_wording`                                           |
| 4   | a report with no distribution says the delta is one draw      | `test_a_report_without_a_distribution_says_the_delta_is_one_draw`                             |
| 5   | both distributions survive `--json`                           | `test_json_carries_both_distributions`                                                        |
| 6   | a malformed `{min, avg, max}` is dropped rather than believed | `spreadOf`'s per-node validator; absence prints as absence                                    |

Criterion 6 is the one inherited from `recoveryOf` in `cortex-eval`: a distribution that is present but wrong
would let a reader price a delta against a spread no run produced.

### 13.144.4 What it changes about everything already registered

- **§13.122.2's ±6-question band is a band on draws, not on means.** The mean over four repetitions is tighter by
  about a factor of two. Every "inside the band" verdict in this document was reached on draws and remains valid
  as stated, but it is not the resolution of a reported mean.
- **§13.133's +1.3 questions** was measured on draws. On the mean it is nearer the resolution, which makes it
  neither confirmed nor refuted — a treatment at that size needs repetitions, not a bigger population.
- **§13.143's verdict does not change, its reason does.** `derive` is refuted as registered (every threshold
  failed) and inert at this resolution (means overlap). The sentence "it lost six questions" was wrong and is
  withdrawn below.

### 13.144.5 The rule this adds

**A paired delta is a claim about two draws; an artifact that carries four repetitions has a mean, and the mean is
what a reader is quoted.** Applied forward: no threshold in this document is set from a first-repetition number,
and any treatment whose predicted effect is smaller than its run's own per-capability range is registered as
"needs repetitions" rather than dispatched against a threshold it cannot reach.

### 13.145 The four repetitions were published as three numbers, and the denominator was the constraint

#### 13.145.1 The defect

`ablation.ts` has held `featureCorrectPerRun` -- a boolean vector per repetition, one entry per question -- since
13.88. It collapsed each capability's per-run **count** into `{min, avg, max}` and dropped the vectors. Every
artifact that has ever left the runner therefore states that MR scored between 81 and 87 out of 121 and cannot
state **which** question moved.

The cost is not cosmetic. Three numbers cannot be recomputed for a population smaller than a capability, and every
ask this campaign has registered in the last four sections is about a population smaller than a capability. A review
pass reaches ten of the 121 MR questions (13.141.1). Ten questions is not a rounding of 121; it is a different
experiment, and the artifact that would have answered it was throwing the denominator away one line before it
computed the summary.

#### 13.145.2 What the artifact now carries

`ablation.featureCorrectByRun` and `ablation.baselineCorrectByRun`: run-major, one string per repetition, one
character per dataset question, `'1'` correct and `'0'` not. 2 kB for the 500-question roster, a character grid
rather than a bitmask so that a reader in `tools/*.mjs` is not a bit-twiddler.

Three properties it is built to have:

- **Omitted at one repetition.** It would be a second copy of `featureCorrect`, and two arrays that must agree are
  two arrays that can disagree -- the reason `correctnessVector` derives rather than stores.
- **Verified, not trusted, by the reader.** `ledger.mjs` refuses a grid whose first row is not the roster's verdicts
  text. `questions[]` is documented as the first repetition, so a grid that fails that comparison is a grid whose
  question order cannot be read; a shifted reading would be arithmetically perfect and about the wrong questions.
- **Readable per declared population.** `--treated <field>=<value>` now cuts the grid as well as the split, through
  one shared `bucketOfQuestion`, so the population the split divides and the population the grid is cut by cannot
  drift into two definitions.

#### 13.145.3 The arithmetic that makes narrowing worth more than repeating

Run `40859499624`'s MR side, four repetitions each: feature 81-87 (avg 83.0), baseline 100-101 (avg 100.75). The
`{min, avg, max}` triple bounds the per-draw spread: with four draws summing to 332 and spanning 81-87, the
distribution is `(81, 82, 82, 87)` or `(81, 81, 83, 87)`, so `sd ≈ 2.35-2.45`. The baseline side sums to 403 and
cannot exceed 101, so it is `(100, 101, 101, 101)`, `sd ≈ 0.43`.

Two comparisons are named separately below, and they are **not** the same instrument. A _within-artifact_ delta
compares the feature side against the reference side of one run, where the reference side is close to deterministic.
A _cross-artifact_ delta compares two dispatches of the **same** memory arm, so both sides carry the full per-draw
spread. Every verdict in this document has been one or the other, and the difference is a factor of 1.4.

| comparison                                       | population | per-draw sd (arm / control) | SE of the 4-vs-4 difference | smallest difference resolved at 80% power |
| ------------------------------------------------ | ---------- | --------------------------- | --------------------------- | ----------------------------------------- |
| within-artifact (feature vs its reference side)  | 121        | 2.45 / 0.43                 | 1.24                        | **4.2 questions** (3.5 pp)                |
| cross-artifact (two dispatches of one arm)       | 121        | 2.45 / 2.45                 | 1.73                        | **5.8 questions** (4.8 pp)                |
| cross-artifact, reachable ten at the corpus rate | 10         | 0.70 / 0.70                 | 0.50                        | **1.7 questions**                         |
| cross-artifact, reachable ten, each a coin flip  | 10         | 1.58 / 1.58                 | 1.12                        | **3.8 questions**                         |

The 80%-power column is `(t_{0.975,6} + t_{0.80,6}) · SE = 3.353 · SE`, with `SE = sqrt(sd_arm²/4 + sd_control²/4)`.

**The row that matters for this campaign's conversion asks is the second one, and it is 5.8, not 4.2.** `recover`
against `bare` is a cross-artifact comparison: both are the memory arm, both carry the 2.45 spread, so the floor is
1.73 · 3.353 = 5.8 questions. `13.141.5`'s registered "+4 of the ten convert" is therefore **below** the resolution
of the mean it is registered against -- not on it. A true +4 would land inside the run's own spread and would be
reported as "not a separation" every time.

Two readings follow, and they are the reason this section exists rather than a note inside 13.144:

1. **Four repetitions are not the binding constraint.** `13.141.5` registered ">= 4 of the ten MR questions convert"
   -- 4 questions against a 5.8-question floor. It is not one draw away from its own resolution; it is **below** it,
   so the registered ask could not have been confirmed on the population it was written for even if it were true.
2. **Narrowing the population buys more than buying repetitions.** Four more repetitions per arm move 5.8 to
   5.8 / sqrt(2) = 4.1 at double the cost and double the wall clock. Reading the ten reachable questions instead
   moves the floor to 1.7-3.8 at **no additional cost**, because the 111 questions that cannot move contribute their
   variance and nothing else.

The corpus rate used in the middle row is derived from the same artifact: `sd² = Σ p_i(1-p_i) = 6.0` over 121
questions gives `p(1-p) ≈ 0.05`, i.e. about 6 MR questions change their answer between draws. The third row is the
worst case, where the ten reachable questions are precisely the unstable ones.

#### 13.145.4 Acceptance criteria, and how each was tested

| #   | criterion                                                                      | test                                                                                                                                |
| --- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 1   | one character per question per repetition, in dataset order                    | `correctness-matrix.test.ts` -- `carries one character per question per repetition, in dataset order`                               |
| 2   | the grid's first row is the roster's verdicts text                             | `agrees with the first-repetition vector`; `ledger.mjs` refuses otherwise (`test_refuses_a_grid_that_does_not_describe_the_roster`) |
| 3   | omitted at one repetition rather than duplicated                               | `omits the field when there is one repetition`                                                                                      |
| 4   | a trailing false is a question, not padding                                    | `does not treat a trailing false as absent`                                                                                         |
| 5   | rows that disagree on length are refused, not padded                           | `test_refuses_a_grid_whose_rows_cover_different_rosters`                                                                            |
| 6   | the per-question read names `always` / `never` / `moved` and the per-draw sd   | `test_reads_each_question_across_the_repetitions`                                                                                   |
| 7   | conversions are counted as questions, in both directions                       | `test_counts_the_questions_that_traded_one_extreme_for_the_other`                                                                   |
| 8   | a fully stable population says so instead of printing a mean it cannot sharpen | `test_says_so_when_narrowing_the_population_bought_nothing`                                                                         |
| 9   | a side without a grid says its repetitions cannot be read                      | `test_a_side_without_a_grid_says_its_repetitions_cannot_be_read`                                                                    |
| 10  | the JSON node and the text come from one function                              | `test_json_carries_the_repetition_summary`                                                                                          |

Two mutations were run against the derivation and both were caught. Publishing only the first repetition reddens
criterion 1. Reversing the mask inside `correctnessMask` reddened **nothing** in the first version of the fixture,
because `'111'` and `'101'` are palindromes -- the alignment was pinned by no test at all. The fixture now flips the
first of four questions and produces `'1111'` / `'0111'`, and the reversal mutation reddens criterion 1. The
palindrome is recorded here rather than quietly fixed: it is the second time this campaign has found a green test
whose fixture could not distinguish the behaviour it claimed to check (13.137.4's `extra` parameter was the first).

#### 13.145.5 What it changes for the in-flight `recover` run and for every ask after it

Run `40883121464` (`review_pass=recover`, tree `ed805b2`) was dispatched before this field existed, so **its
artifact will carry no grid** and `13.141.5` has to be read on the whole-MR mean -- and, because it is a
cross-artifact comparison, the 5.8-question floor rather than 4.2. That is not a reason to cancel it: its control
(`40859499624`) is matched on everything except the two commits that intentionally differ. But the read has to be
stated before it lands, so that the number cannot be given a meaning it does not have: **any MR delta below six
questions is inside this pair's own spread**, and a result at 87.0 against 83.0 is "four questions, which this
instrument cannot separate", not "recover bought four questions".

#### 13.145.6 The ten are measurable but not yet addressable, and that is the next instrument

13.145.3's middle and bottom rows price a population the artifact cannot currently name. `--treated` cuts on a
**record field**, and the record carries no marker saying "the recovery pass acted on this question":

| what the artifact carries                                                              | what it does not                                                                             |
| -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `capability: 'MR'` -- 121 questions                                                    | which of them bare-declined                                                                  |
| `recovery: {attempted, answered}` -- two **counts** for the whole run                  | which questions those counts came from                                                       |
| `answer: null` + `rawOutput` -- per question, and a decline is inferable from the pair | a field that says so, and no way to say "declined in the **control**" as a `--treated` value |

So the 1.2-2.7 column is arithmetic about a population that would need one of two additions before a run could
report it:

1. **A per-question marker on the arm side** (`recoveryAttempted`, `recoveryAnswered`), taken as the delta of the
   existing `recoveryCensus()` around one answer call. Arm-side is the same side `--treated` already reads, so the
   tool needs no new semantics -- only the field. This is the smaller change and it answers "did the mechanism act
   here", which is what a **mechanism** ask needs.
2. **A control-side predicate** (`--treated control.answer=declined`), for asks whose population is defined by the
   control's behaviour rather than the arm's. Larger: it introduces a side into the split's ontology, which the
   current `bucketOfQuestion` deliberately does not have.

The registered ask is therefore **not** "read the ten" but "**record which ten**". Until one of the two lands, every
conversion ask on this axis is read at the whole-capability resolution in 13.145.3's first row, and 4.2 questions is
the honest floor for it.

The rule this adds: **any ask registered against fewer than a whole capability must state its population and its
resolution in questions before it is dispatched, and must name the artifact field that population is addressable
through** -- a third clause, because the first two are satisfiable by arithmetic alone and this section is the case
where the arithmetic was written before the field existed. 4.2 whole-MR was never printed anywhere in this document until
now, and three registered asks (`13.133`'s +1.3, `13.141.5`'s 4-of-10, `13.143`'s thresholds) were written against
thresholds that this arithmetic says they could not have reached on the population they were written for.

### 13.146 The ten are addressable now: a census delta rather than a fourth counter

#### 13.146.1 What 13.145.6 left open

`ablation.recovery` and `ablation.bareRetry` are `{attempted, answered}` for the **whole run**. Every
conversion ask registered against those mechanisms therefore names a population the artifact cannot
address, and 13.145.3's 1.7-3.8-question column was arithmetic about a set of questions nothing could
point at.

The fix could have been a flag inside the product, reset per question. It was rejected for a reason worth
writing down: **a stateful beacon is stale for every question the mechanism did not touch.** `#lastReview`
is reset inside `#promptSessionAware`, which only the multi-session route enters -- so a flat question read
immediately after an MR question reports the MR question's value. The same shape in a new field would have
produced a per-question marker that is wrong for 379 of 500 questions, and wrong in the direction that looks
like a hit.

#### 13.146.2 The instrument

`traceReviewMechanisms(system, trace)` wraps the feature system and records, per question, whether
`recoveryCensus()` advanced across that one answer:

- **A delta, not a counter.** The product already states this fact three times (`abstentionReasons`,
  `bareRetryCensus`, `recoveryCensus`); a fourth counter is a fourth thing to drift.
- **A prototype chain, not a spread.** `Object.create(system)` and not `{ ...system }`: a class instance
  keeps its methods on the prototype, so a spread would copy no method at all and `isSessionAware` -- which
  tests for `answerSessions` -- would see a flat-only system. One test asserts the member survives.
- **Every `answer*` member, by prefix.** Seven routing members today; a prefix rather than a list, so a
  member added later is covered rather than silently untraced.
- **Absent when the instrument is absent.** No `recoveryCensus` returns the system **unchanged**; a census
  that throws is treated as absent, checked once and then abandoned rather than retried per question. Both
  cases write **no field**, because `false` would say the mechanism did not fire on a run where the
  instrument that would have known does not exist -- and `--treated` would then classify it as `untouched`
  instead of `unknown`.
- **Two fields, not one.** A retry that fired and declined again is `recoveryAttempted` without
  `recoveryAnswered`, and that half is what says the mechanism ran rather than which way it went.

The record fields are `recoveryAttempted` / `recoveryAnswered`, forwarded through `report-write.ts`'s
rebuild for the reason `promptChars` is: a field the rebuild does not carry is a field a reduction silently
drops, and this one is the only per-question statement of which questions a review pass reached.

#### 13.146.3 Acceptance criteria, and how each was tested

All seven are end-to-end, through `runCortexMemoryArm`, in `bench-memory-arm-census.test.ts`:

| #   | criterion                                                         | test                                                                                                                                                             |
| --- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 1   | the trace varies **by question**, not by run                      | `marks which question the pass reached, not only how many times it ran`                                                                                          |
| 2   | a retry that fired and declined is `attempted` without `answered` | `records a retry that fired and declined again as attempted without answered`                                                                                    |
| 3   | a system with no census writes **neither** field                  | `writes neither field for a system that cannot be traced`                                                                                                        |
| 4   | a throwing census is absent, not a failed run                     | `treats a throwing accessor as absent rather than failing the run`                                                                                               |
| 5   | a constant census marks nothing                                   | `renders zero attempts as not-applicable rather than as a share of nothing` (the census tests above, unchanged, now also see `attempted: false` on every record) |
| 6   | the wrapper does not drop `answerSessions`                        | pinned by the existing session-aware arm tests, which would fail as a flat-only system                                                                           |
| 7   | the count and the trace cannot disagree                           | both are read from the same accessor in the same function; criterion 4 is the case where they would have                                                         |

Criterion 1's fixture is the load-bearing one. The first version of these tests used a **one-question**
dataset, where every per-question field has exactly one value and an implementation that wrote a run-level
number on every record would pass. The fixture now advances the census only on the second of two questions,
so `[false, true]` is the only passing answer -- and a trace that read the final count would produce
`[true, true]`, which is the defect with a plausible shape.

Two things were caught during the change rather than after it, and both are worth recording.

**The unguarded wrapper broke a rule the arm already followed.** `bench-memory-arm-census.test.ts` required a
throwing `recoveryCensus` to leave the counts absent; the first version of the trace propagated the throw and
turned that test into a stack trace inside `runBenchmark`. On a real dispatch that is a 2h20m run ending with
no artifact. It was found because the wrapper sits on the accessor the count already reads.

**The export census refused the change.** `traceReviewMechanisms` and `ReviewMechanismTrace` were exported so
a unit test could import them, and `pnpm check`'s `census:check` failed with `2 NEW orphan(s) not in the
baseline` -- correctly, because an export no production code calls is an invitation for the next reader to
import it. The repair was not to add it to `tools/export-census-baseline.json`; it was to **drop the export
and move the tests through the public seam**, which is how the one-question fixture above got found: the
direct unit tests had been satisfied by a single question, and the arm-level ones could not be.

#### 13.146.4 What it changes

`--treated recoveryAttempted=true` now cuts the record set to the questions the pass actually reached, which
turns 13.145.3's third and fourth rows from arithmetic into a reading **on the next dispatch**: no artifact
written before this field exists carries it, and `ledger.mjs` reports the missing side as `unknown` rather
than as untouched.

It also gives every future mechanism ask the same seam. `bareRetryCensus()` has the same shape, and a watch
that fires on one question and not the next is the generic case -- the wrapper is keyed on the accessor, so
a second mechanism is one more wrapper and no change to the record type.

## 13.147 What one dispatch buys, read from the code because there is no invoice to read

§13.140 registered the instrument that prices a run and §13.142 settled one prediction without spending a
