call. Neither answers the question a reader of the bill asks first: **which call is the expensive one, and is
any of it buying nothing?** That is answerable from the source alone, and this section answers it from the
source -- with the reach of each answer in questions, because "the prompt is 48,000 characters" is a fact
about a constant and "eleven thousand questions are answered per dispatch" is a fact about a bill.

### 13.147.1 The call graph, counted

Every provider request in the registered configuration (`ablation_runs: 4`, `review_pass: bare`,
`rerank: none`, `query_expansion: none`, `self_consistency: none`), per arm per 500-question pass:

| call                     | built at                                | count                                                                      | prompt size                                                                             | reusable prefix                                                      |
| ------------------------ | --------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| first-pass answer        | `#answerWithBareRetry` -> `buildPrompt` | 500                                                                        | `cortex_memory_max_prompt_chars` = 48,000, and §13.139 measures 468 of 500 at 95% of it | none: the prompt is question-specific from its first evidence line   |
| bare-decline retry       | `buildRetryPrompt`                      | 21 (feature arm only, §13.94)                                              | the first pass's window plus a longer instruction                                       | its whole evidence block is the head of the first prompt (§13.147.4) |
| abstention recovery      | `buildRecoveryPrompt`                   | **10** when `review_pass: recover` (§13.141.2, 8.25 measured in §13.149.1) | the reader's own Step 1 list, no evidence re-sent                                       | not applicable                                                       |
| answer audit             | `buildAuditPrompt`                      | 500 when `review_pass: audit`                                              | the window again                                                                        | not in this configuration                                            |
| answer-equivalence judge | `buildJudgePrompt`                      | at most 500, less its own cache                                            | question + predicted + expected, a few hundred characters                               | fully: keyed on the triple                                           |
| cross-encoder rerank     | `LLMReranker.score`                     | 0                                                                          | --                                                                                      | registered `none`                                                    |
| query expansion          | --                                      | 0                                                                          | --                                                                                      | registered `none`                                                    |

So one dispatch of this arm issues **4,000 first-pass answer calls** (four repetitions, two sides), **84
retries**, and **at most 1,000 judge calls**. The judge is nearly free twice over and both reasons are
deliberate: its prompt is two short strings and a question, and `judge.ts` caches verdicts process-wide on the
`(question, predicted, expected)` triple -- which repetitions 2-4 mostly hit, because the flip rate on
untouched questions is 7.08% (§13.135) and 92.92% of a repetition's answers are the previous repetition's
answer verbatim. A repetition therefore pays for its answer prompts and almost nothing for its grading.

**Measured, after the first bill arrived** (`40883121464`): 4,000 first-pass calls exactly, **128** retries (95
bare + 33 recovery, both feature-side only) and therefore **1,628** judge calls, so the judge cache hit 59.3%
rather than the ~93% predicted from the flip rate. The two retry estimates in the table were per-pass numbers
(21 bare) and the measured rates are 23.75 bare and 8.25 recovery per pass; the recovery row's 10 replaces a
13-17 that was the capability census before §13.141.2 removed the six questions on routes the pass is not
wired into. §13.148.5 decomposes the bill and §13.149.1 reads the recovery population.

**The whole bill is the first-pass answer prompt.** Everything else in the table is a rounding error against
4,000 x ~11,400 tokens, which is why the rest of this section is about that one call and about whether
repetitions pay for it more than once.

### 13.147.2 The arithmetic, cold

§13.139 measures the roster's **median** `promptChars` at 46,851 on the 48,000 ceiling -- not the threshold, the
middle question, with 468 of 500 at or above 95% of it and the largest 409 characters short. At four characters
per token that is **11,713 tokens**; 4,000 calls make **46.9M prompt tokens** per dispatch, against roughly 0.2M
completion tokens (the answer is a line or a short list) and 0.15M judge tokens.

The 4.0 is an assumption, and it is the one number here that the artifact retires rather than confirms:
`llmUsage.promptTokens` divided by the roster's `promptChars` is the measured ratio, and a ratio far from 4.0
would mean the prompt is not what the roster says it is. It is not exact in either direction -- `promptChars`
describes the **first** prompt only, so the division understates the ratio by the retry's share, which
§13.147.1 puts at 84 calls of 4,000.

### 13.147.3 Prediction 2 is about to be answered by the wrong variable, and the repair goes on record first

The `recover` dispatch now in flight is the first artifact carrying `llmUsage`. It will report the three
numbers §13.140.5 predicts, and two of those predictions cannot be read the way they are written:

**Prediction 1's band cannot tell one run from four.** One 500-question pass, two sides, cold: 1,000 x 11,400
= **11.4M**, inside the registered 10-14M. Four repetitions with repeats served from a prefix cache:
11.4M + 3 x 11.4M x 0.1 = **14.8M**, also inside it. A total inside the band is therefore compatible with both
"every call paid full price once" and "three quarters of the prompt tokens were billed at a tenth", and the
band must not be read as evidence for either.

**Prediction 2 is stated about ordering and will be measured against repetition.** Its premise is that the
only reusable prefix is the fixed instruction block, "a few hundred tokens of 47,000 characters" -- true
_within_ a pass. But a dispatch runs four passes, and passes 2-4 send **byte-identical requests**: `now` is
fixed at construction (`bench/run-ablation.ts` evaluates `Date.now()` once, before either system answers
anything), retrieval is deterministic over a cached embedding store, and the reader runs at temperature 0
(§13.119). A repetition is not a similar prompt, it is the same prompt. If the provider serves prefixes at all,
the expected share over a four-run dispatch is near 3/4 -- and that number would say nothing about ordering.

So prediction 2's threshold is retained and its **interpretation** is decomposed, before the reading:

| share      | what it means                                                       | what follows                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| ---------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| under 5%   | no repetition reuse _and_ no ordering win                           | repetitions cost what §13.145.2 assumed they cost; moving a stable block to the front is settled negative, and prediction 2 stands as written                                                                       |
| 60-80%     | repetitions are reused and ordering is invisible from this artifact | the **marginal** repetition is about a tenth of the prompt, so "eight repetitions cost double" is wrong and the resolution arithmetic must be restated before the next repetition decision; ordering stays untested |
| 20% to 60% | neither story fits                                                  | the instrument or the provider is doing something neither this section nor §13.140.2 describes, and per-pass spend is needed to localise it                                                                         |

**Prediction 4, registered here and before the artifact exists:** the share falls in the 60-80% band, because
three of every four answer calls in a dispatch are exact repeats of a prompt the same job has already sent.

The instrument that would settle all three readings at once is **per-pass spend** -- an `llmUsage` delta around
each of the eight passes rather than around the ablation -- and it is deliberately _not_ built yet: if the
share lands in the top band it answers the repetition question on its own, and if it lands in the bottom band
per-pass spend would be a second measurement of a fact already known. The middle band is the only one that
needs it, and that is the reason to wait rather than to guess.

### 13.147.4 The retry re-sent a window the first pass had refused, and its docstring said it did not

`buildRetryPrompt`'s docstring states the contract: _"The evidence and the question are rendered exactly as
the first pass rendered them, so the only difference between the two calls is the instruction."_
`#answerWithBareRetry` passed it `kept` -- the window the **route admitted** -- rather than
`assembled.carried`, the set the **first prompt carried**. On a question where the budget binds, those are
different objects, and the retry was built from the larger one.

Measured on the fixture in `bare-decline-retry.test.ts` (eight turns, a 520-character budget): the first
prompt is 520 characters and its evidence ends mid-turn, because `fitToBudget` clips at a character boundary;
the retry was **1,024 characters**, and every one of those extra 504 characters was evidence the first pass had
just refused to send. It is the only call in the pipeline with no ceiling on it at all.

Three things are now asserted rather than described, and each of them fails on the pre-fix code:

1. **It drops what the first pass dropped.** The retry carries every line the first prompt carried and none it
   did not. (The fixture must bind -- the test asserts `dropped.length > 0` -- or it measures a prompt that
   fits and proves nothing.)
2. **Its evidence block is a byte prefix of the first prompt.** `render(prefix)` is a prefix of `render(all)`
   whenever the produced text is contiguous from the start, which is the property `wholeTurnsIn` already
   relies on. Pre-fix the block was _longer_ than the first prompt and no provider could serve a byte of it;
   post-fix the shared head is exactly what a prefix cache reads.
3. **It never carries more of the window than the call it corrects** -- and, separately, its instruction block
   is _longer_ than the contract's (369 characters against 145 on the fixture), which is pinned so that a
   future comparison of total lengths cannot be mistaken for the evidence comparison that means something.

**What this is worth, honestly: nothing at all on the configuration that is running, and that is the finding.**
§13.139's distribution says no question on the roster exceeds the ceiling -- zero at 48,000, the largest at
47,591 -- so `fitToBudget` never fires at the registered budget and `carried` and `kept` are the same array on
all 500 questions. The defect is **latent at 48,000 and live at 24,000**: the product default every run before
§13.82 used was 24,000 against a median window of 46,851, which means on that configuration a retry re-sent
**nearly twice the ceiling** it was correcting, on every question that retried. The reason to fix it is not
today's bill. It is that a dispatchable ceiling is one `--set` away from being that configuration again, and the
retry would then answer from a window no other call in the pipeline was allowed to see.

**And the retry still has no budget of its own**, which is registered as _unchanged_ rather than as an
oversight: post-fix it is 669 characters against a 520-character budget, and the excess is the instruction.
Spending a ceiling on the treatment would truncate the treatment; the evidence is bounded by the first pass,
and that is the part the ceiling was ever meant to bound.

### 13.147.5 What none of this licences

- **§13.140.6 stands unchanged.** The control arm is not cached, the repetitions are not cut, and the window is
  not shrunk: the first two destroy the noise floor and the third is the arm's independent variable.
- **No prices.** `usage.ts` refuses to hold a rate card and this section does not introduce one. Token counts
  are facts the provider published; a currency figure is a fact about a contract, and a stale contract
  denominated in money survives review in a way a stale count cannot.
- **No conclusion about ordering.** Prediction 2's third row is the only one that would licence an ordering
  experiment, and it is the one row that cannot arrive from a four-run dispatch.

### 13.147.6 Acceptance criteria

| #   | criterion                                                                              | test                                                                                                                     |
| --- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| 1   | the retry carries what the first pass carried and drops what it dropped                | `bare-decline-retry.test.ts`, eight-turn fixture with a binding budget                                                   |
| 2   | its evidence block is a byte prefix of the first prompt                                | same file, `startsWith` on the block                                                                                     |
| 3   | it never carries more evidence than the call it corrects                               | same file, evidence lengths compared                                                                                     |
| 4   | the reason a total-length comparison would be wrong is pinned                          | same file, instruction lengths compared in the opposite direction                                                        |
| 5   | a reasoned decline is still not retried, and an answer never is                        | pre-existing tests, unchanged                                                                                            |
| 6   | the abstention route is still untouched                                                | pre-existing test, unchanged                                                                                             |
| 7   | the spend readout prints what the artifact states, and derives the per-pass call count | `test_readout_arm_run.py`, `TestTheProviderSpend`                                                                        |
| 8   | a report with no `llmUsage` is an absence, not a zero-spend run                        | same class: `--spend` exits 2 and says the artifact predates the instrument                                              |
| 9   | a corrupt block is refused rather than printed                                         | same class: a hit above its prompt, more unpriced calls than calls, a negative count, and a `bool` where a count belongs |
| 10  | the cache share is read against the three registered bands                             | same class: 0, 0.10, 0.40 and 0.70 of the prompt each produce their own verdict                                          |

Criterion 2 is the one that constrains the future: it is the only assertion in the suite that would fail if a
later refactor rebuilt the retry from turns again, and it is stated in the currency the provider charges in --
bytes at the head of the request.

## 13.148 `recover` converted one question per run, which is a sixth of what this instrument can see

`40883121464` landed at 15:48Z on 2026-10-29 after 2h14m, and it is the first artifact in this campaign that
carries `llmUsage`. It also closes P0. This section reads it against its control and then reads its bill.

### 13.148.1 The comparison is one field, and the artifacts agree on all 23 of the others

|                                             | control `40751394094`                                 | treatment `40883121464` |
| ------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------- |
| `reviewPass`                                | `bare`                                                | `recover`               |
| every other field of `memoryArmConfig`      | identical (23 of 24)                                  | identical (23 of 24)    |
| `promptChars` median / mean over the roster | 46,851.5 / 46,622                                     | 46,851.5 / 46,622       |
| `evidenceTurns` median / max                | 417.5 / 616                                           | 417.5 / 616             |
| reader                                      | `deepseek:deepseek-chat`, thinking disabled, `temp=0` | same                    |

The two rosters are **byte-identical in every window statistic**, which is the internal control this register
asks for before any cross-artifact comparison: the treatment changed what the reader was asked a second time,
and nothing about what it was shown the first time.

### 13.148.2 On MR the means are equal, and the register's floor is 5.8 questions

| capability | control min / mean / max | treatment min / mean / max | Δ mean (questions) |
| ---------- | ------------------------ | -------------------------- | ------------------ |
| IE         | 139 / 140.25 / 142       | 141 / 141.50 / 142         | **+1.25**          |
| **MR**     | **83 / 86.50 / 89**      | **85 / 86.50 / 88**        | **0.00**           |
| KU         | 61 / 62.75 / 64          | 62 / 63.50 / 67            | +0.75              |
| TR         | 100 / 102.50 / 105       | 102 / 103.75 / 105         | +1.25              |
| ABS        | 29 / 29.00 / 29          | 29 / 29.25 / 30            | +0.25              |
| overall    | 83.4 / 84.20 / 84.8      | 84.4 / 84.90 / 85.6        | +3.50              |

Three things have to be read together, and none of them is the +0.70 points.

**1. MR did not move at all.** Mean 86.50 on both sides, and the ranges overlap (83-89 against 85-88). Against
the 5.8-question cross-artifact floor of §13.145.3 this is not "below resolution" in the sense of a small positive
number that might be real -- it is **zero**, and the honest statement is that no gain was observed at all.

**2. The routes the pass cannot reach moved by as much as the route it can.** §13.141.1 states the pass lives in
`answerSessions`, so `IE`, `KU`, `TR` and `ABS` are byte-identical by construction. They moved +1.25, +0.75, +1.25
and +0.25 -- in questions, 10 bought and 5 sold, a net of +5 that is the whole roster's net. That is a measurement
of **this pair of dispatches' own churn on questions nothing touched**, about one question per capability, and it
is the number any future increment has to beat before its own capability count means anything.

On the one route the pass _can_ reach, the split is sharper and §13.149 reads it: 2 of its 10 questions converted
and 5 of the other 111 did, so the treated and untreated questions converted at 20.0% and 20.8%. The mean is zero
not because the mechanism did nothing visible but because **a mean over 121 questions cannot see two**.

**3. The reference pipeline moved further than the treatment did.** Its overall mean fell 45.15% -> 44.10%
(**-5.25 questions**) and its MR mean fell 107.5 -> 103.0 (**-4.5 questions**) between the two dispatches, with
no field in either artifact to explain it -- the reference pipeline's own configuration is recorded nowhere.
This is not a defect of the treatment; it is the empirical answer to "why is the floor 5.8": **an untreated side
of the same experiment drifted 4.5 questions on MR.**

### 13.148.3 Paired, question by question, the flow is 14 and the net is 0

Means can hide a cancellation, so the same comparison is read as transitions. The control's roster and this
one are paired by `questionId`, first repetition against first repetition (neither artifact carries the
per-run grid, which shipped after both were dispatched):

| capability | n       | bought | sold  | net   |
| ---------- | ------- | ------ | ----- | ----- |
| IE         | 150     | 3      | 1     | +2    |
| **MR**     | **121** | **7**  | **7** | **0** |
| KU         | 72      | 1      | 0     | +1    |
| TR         | 127     | 6      | 4     | +2    |
| ABS        | 30      | 0      | 0     | 0     |
| roster     | 500     | 17     | 12    | +5    |

**MR's gross flow is 14 questions out of 121 and its net is zero.** The treatment is not "small"; it is
indistinguishable, at this sample size, from the reader answering the same questions twice. And the two largest
nets in the table (+2 IE, +2 TR) sit on capabilities the pass provably cannot reach.

`node tools/ledger.mjs --control <control> --across recover=<this>` prints this table and the per-capability
range overlap from the two artifacts; the run it reads is named on its first line.

### 13.148.4 The mechanism's own census reproduces its population and falsifies its conversion floor

|                                         | registered (§13.141.5, after the route correction) | measured over 4 runs | per run  |
| --------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------- | -------------------- | -------- |
| declines that contradict their own list | **10** per run (§13.141.2)                         | 33                   | **8.25** |
| returned an answer                      | "at least 4 of the 10"                             | 4                    | **1.0**  |

Two things are true of this table and only one of them is a failure.

**The population is reproduced, not halved.** 8.25 consultations per run against a registered 10 is 0.82x, and
the register's own decline census moves between repetitions (the control's first recorded repetition has 12 MR
declines of which 10 carry a list). §13.149.1 recomputes the census from the control with the product's own
predicates and gets 10, 1.60 mean items and 4 counting questions -- §13.128.1's table to the digit.

**The conversion floor is missed by half.** The pass _answered_ 4 of its 33 consultations, so it converted at
most 4 questions over four runs against a registered floor of 4 per run. Since answering is necessary for
converting, `answered` bounds conversions from above and the falsification needs no judge. §13.149.3 reads the
conversions themselves, question by question, and the verdict there is stronger than "below the floor".

The bare ladder's check belongs beside this: 95 retries in the treatment against 92 in the control. §13.141.1
predicted that the pre-repair derivation would have withdrawn 92 consultations into this dispatch; 95 says the
union repair held, and §13.141.3's test is why.

**What this subsection said first, and why it was wrong.** Three numbers and one narrative were wrong here, and
§13.149.5 records them: 13-17 (the capability census before §13.141.2, not the registered population), "5 of the
16" (retired by §13.141.5 in favour of 4 of the 10), "the 5 counting questions" (that is the sixteen's count; the
ten have 4), and the claim that the two passes "claim the same question in different orders on different routes",
which contradicts the route table §13.141.1 established and §13.141.4 criterion 7 asserts by counting calls: the
ladder is not wired into `multi-session` and the recovery pass is wired into nothing else, so they cannot compete
for a question at all.

### 13.148.5 The bill, and what it settles

| field                                      | value          |
| ------------------------------------------ | -------------- |
| calls that returned a response             | 5,756          |
| of those, no `usage` block                 | **0**          |
| prompt tokens                              | **37,100,936** |
| completion tokens                          | 365,791        |
| prompt tokens served from the prefix cache | 2,402,211      |
| prefix-cache share                         | **6.47%**      |

The call count decomposes exactly: 4,000 first-pass answer calls (four repetitions, two sides, 500 questions),
128 retries (95 bare + 33 recovery, both on the feature side only), and therefore **1,628 judge calls** -- a
judge-cache hit rate of 59.3%, not the ~93% §13.147.1 predicted from the 7.08% flip rate.

| prediction                                | registered | measured   | verdict                                                                                     |
| ----------------------------------------- | ---------- | ---------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| §13.140.5 #1, prompt tokens               | 10M-14M    | 37.1M      | **falsified**, 2.65x the top of the band                                                    |
| §13.140.5 #2, prefix-cache share under 5% | <5%        | 6.47%      | **falsified** by 1.47 points, and the "ordering is a lever" clause (>20%) is not met either |
| §13.140.5 #3, `unpricedCalls`             | 0          | 0 of 5,756 | **confirmed**                                                                               |
| §13.147.3 #4, the share lands in 60-80%   | 60-80%     | 6.47%      | **falsified**                                                                               |

Prediction 1 was already amended in §13.147.3 before this artifact existed, and the amendment is what makes the
reading clean rather than surprising: 37.1M is what a four-pass dispatch costs, and the band was a one-pass
number. **§13.147.2's cold model is 30% high and cannot be corrected from this artifact**: it predicts 48.4M for
the answer side, the measured total for both sides plus the judge is 37.1M, and the gap is either a
characters-per-token ratio above 4.0 or a reference window smaller than the feature's -- a two-unknown division
that §13.148.6 states as a bracket rather than a number.

**Prediction 4 is falsified, and the 6.47% answers the cost question on its own.** The attribution of the credit
is a hypothesis and is marked as one: the retry path re-sends its first pass's evidence seconds later, so 128
retries x ~8,900 tokens is about **1.14M, or 47% of the credit, and that part is within-pass by construction** --
and a fixed preamble on the reference side is the plausible source of much of the rest. **No across-pass credit is
demonstrated**, but none is excluded either, which is exactly the gap §13.147.3 registered per-pass spend for.

What the number settles does not depend on that attribution, and this is the airtight form:

- **A repetition costs at least 93.5% of a full prompt.** The whole cache credit is 6.47% of the prompt bill, and
  a lower bound on the within-pass part of it already exists (the retry path), so whatever the across-pass share
  turns out to be, it is at most 6.47% and the repetition price cannot move by more than that. §13.145.2's cost
  column stands, and "buy more repetitions to beat the noise floor" is expensive in the way it was assumed to be.
  **Erratum (`§13.168.8`):** 6.47% is the share of prompt _tokens_ served from cache, not the share of the bill
  the cache removes, because a cached token still bills at a tenth. Under the price model `§13.147.3` registered,
  the money credit is `0.9 × 6.47% = 5.82%`, so the bound is **94.2%, not 93.5%** — the sentence above is
  conservative rather than wrong, and the conclusion it supports does not move by the correction.
- **Per-pass spend is the instrument that would close the residual 6.47%**, and it is worth building for the
  attribution rather than for the decision: the decision it could change is bounded by six percent of a bill.
- **Prompt ordering is settled negative, by derivation rather than by a run.** The only prefix stable across
  questions is the instruction block, and on the longest route it is 1,591 characters -- **3.41%** of a
  46,622-character prompt, measured by building the prompt (`buildSessionPrompt` with one session: 1,605
  characters, of which 14 are evidence). Moving it to the front would put 3.41% of the prompt at a tenth of the
  rate: **a saving of about 3%**, on a dispatch that costs four figures' worth of tokens. There is no experiment
  to run here.

### 13.148.6 What the bill cannot say, which is why it cannot be checked further

Two gaps, both exposed by the reading rather than predicted by it.

**The bill is not split by side.** One `llmUsage` delta covers both arms, the judge and every retry. The feature
side alone carries 93.3M characters over its four passes (46,622 x 500 x 4), so the measured 37.1M tokens imply
**at least 2.5 characters per token**; if the reference side's window were the same size the total would be
186.5M characters and the ratio 5.0. The artifact carries neither the reference's window nor a per-side split, so
the ratio is a **bracket of 2.5 to 5.1 and not a number**, and §13.147.2's 4.0 sits inside it: the artifact
neither confirms nor refutes that constant. What it does refute is the arithmetic built on it -- a 4.0-based cold
model of this dispatch is 4,128 x 11,713 = 48.4M tokens, and the measured total is 37.1M, so either the ratio is
above 4 on this roster or the reference side's window is smaller than the feature's. Both are plausible, neither
is readable from this artifact, and a per-side delta settles it in one field.

**The reference pipeline's configuration is not in the artifact at all.** Only its `name` and its `metrics` are.
That is why its 4.5-question MR drift cannot be attributed: a reader cannot tell a slower run from a changed
window from a different retry policy, and the one thing a cross-artifact floor needs is the ability to say the
control did not move for a reason.

Both are one field each -- a per-side `llmUsage` delta, and the reference pipeline's `memoryArmConfig` -- and both
are registered here rather than built, for the reason §13.147.3 gives: a measurement that no decision is waiting
on is a measurement that ships untested.

### 13.148.7 What the next dispatch has to be

P0 closes as **not separated, with zero observed effect and a mechanism whose population converts at the
reader's own rate** (§13.149.3). Three consequences, in the order they bind:

1. **`recover` closes, and it is not worth a second dispatch on its own account.** §13.149.3 measures its
   population's conversion at 20.0% against a same-route base rate of 20.8%, so the honest reading of the
   registered "4 of 10" is not "underpowered" but "the bar was set above a rate the mechanism does not have". A
   second dispatch would be measuring the same base rate with four more pairings.
2. **The next dispatch that measures anything on MR must carry the per-run grid and the per-question reach
   marks**, because this pair carries neither and the paired reading above is therefore one pairing of sixteen
   possible ones. §13.149.6 states the design the grid makes possible: the pass's population converted against
   **itself** in a pairing where it did not fire, which is the only counterfactual that does not lean on another
   capability's rate.
3. **The 5.8-question floor now has an empirical anchor**: an untreated side drifted 4.5 questions on MR between
   two dispatches whose recorded fields are identical. §13.145.3's arithmetic and the reference's behaviour agree,
   which is the first time that floor has been checked against a number rather than derived.

## 13.149 The recovery pass converted its population at the reader's own rate, which is what no mechanism looks like

§13.148 read `40883121464` as a dispatch: means, paired flow, bill. It deliberately did not read the one quantity
this pass was built to move, because the artifact's record cannot be asked for it directly -- the population is a
**predicate over a reply**, not a field, and the treatment's own record overwrites the reply that made a question
reachable. This section builds the instrument that reads it, runs it on this pair, and reports what the pass
actually did to the ten questions it can reach.

The answer is not "it moved one question per run". It is **two of ten, against a base rate that expects 2.08 of
ten**, which is the reading a mechanism has to beat to exist.

### 13.149.1 The population, recomputed with the product's predicates

`tools/recovery-reach.mjs` reads the control and calls `declinedItems` and `asksForCount` from `cortex-memory` --
the same functions §13.128.1 counted with -- and prints the census by capability beside the route each capability
answers on, taken from `evidenceRouteOf` rather than restated:

| capability | route               | questions | declines | listed | counting | mean items | reached |
| ---------- | ------------------- | --------: | -------: | -----: | -------: | ---------: | ------- |
| IE         | `flat`              |       150 |        1 |      0 |        0 |       0.00 | no      |
| **MR**     | **`multi-session`** |   **121** |   **12** | **10** |    **4** |   **1.60** | **yes** |
| KU         | `knowledge-update`  |        72 |        2 |      1 |        0 |       2.00 | no      |
| TR         | `temporal`          |       127 |        8 |      5 |        1 |       3.40 | no      |
| ABS        | `abstention`        |        30 |       29 |      0 |        0 |       0.00 | no      |
| roster     |                     |       500 |       52 |     16 |        5 |            | **10**  |

**This is §13.128.1's table to the digit** -- 16 questions in total, 10 of them on the one route the pass is
wired into, mean 1.6 items on MR against a gold count of 3 to 10. A register whose population could not be
reproduced two sections after it was counted would have a denominator nobody could check.

### 13.149.2 Why the population has to come from the control, and what that costs

`memory.ts` keeps the **last** thing the reader said when the pass consults a question and loses: the retry's own
decline, which carries no list because the recovery prompt does not ask for one. Read from the treatment, the
population therefore disappears:

|                         | MR nulls | of those, carrying a Step 1 list |
| ----------------------- | -------: | -------------------------------: |
| control `40751394094`   |       12 |                           **10** |
| treatment `40883121464` |       10 |                            **0** |

Two questions answered, eight declined a second time, and the two honest declines -- and **every trace of which
question was reachable is gone**. The tool takes the population from the control for that reason, refuses a
control whose population is empty, and refuses a population question the treatment does not carry; the second
refusal is what stops an unpaired question's "no change" from being fabricated.

The field that fixes this for future artifacts is `recoveryAttempted` (§13.146), which records the reach on the
record itself. It does **not** replace this reading: the registration defined the population on the control's
decline census, and a population recomputed from the treated side answers a different question -- "what did the
pass consult" against "what could it have consulted". Both are worth having; only the second is the registered
denominator.

### 13.149.3 Two of ten, against a base rate that expects 2.08

The ten questions, paired by id, with the answer the treatment returned:

| question   | items | counting | control | treatment | moved      | answer  |
| ---------- | ----: | -------- | ------- | --------- | ---------- | ------- |
| `dd2973ad` |     2 | no       | wrong   | **right** | **bought** | `2 AM`  |
| `9aaed6a3` |     1 | no       | wrong   | **right** | **bought** | `$0.75` |
| `60bf93ed` |     1 | yes      | wrong   | wrong     | unchanged  | decline |
| `e6041065` |     1 | no       | wrong   | wrong     | unchanged  | decline |
| `d905b33f` |     1 | no       | wrong   | wrong     | unchanged  | decline |
| `a4996e51` |     2 | yes      | wrong   | wrong     | unchanged  | decline |
| `a1cc6108` |     1 | no       | wrong   | wrong     | unchanged  | decline |
| `73d42213` |     2 | no       | wrong   | wrong     | unchanged  | decline |
| `d6062bb9` |     2 | yes      | wrong   | wrong     | unchanged  | decline |
| `37f165cf` |     3 | yes      | wrong   | wrong     | unchanged  | decline |

Two converted. Both are non-counting questions, and both are the shape the retry is supposed to fix: the reader
had listed the relevant item and declined anyway, and being shown its own list produced the answer.

The question a conversion count cannot answer on its own is **what the same ten questions would have done without
the pass**, and this pairing has a measurement for that. Every question on this route that the control answered
wrongly is a question the reader could have got right on a second draw, and the pairing shows the rate:

| group                 | questions | wrong in the control | wrong -> right |      rate |
| --------------------- | --------: | -------------------: | -------------: | --------: |
| the pass's population |        10 |                   10 |          **2** | **20.0%** |
| same route, untouched |       111 |                   24 |              5 | **20.8%** |
| the whole route       |       121 |                   34 |              7 |     20.6% |
| IE                    |       150 |                   10 |              3 |     30.0% |
| TR                    |       127 |                   27 |              6 |     22.2% |
| KU                    |        72 |                   11 |              1 |      9.1% |
| ABS                   |        30 |                    1 |              0 |      0.0% |

**The treated questions converted at the untreated rate.** 20.0% against 20.8%, and the expected number of
conversions under the base rate is 2.08 -- the measurement is 2, to two significant figures the mean of the
distribution it is being compared against. `P(X >= 2 | 2.08) = 0.62`: the observed count is the _most_ likely
outcome of a reader that never received the treatment.

Three consequences, and the third is the one that changes the roadmap:

- **The pass is a second sample in effect.** Its own docstring argues the opposite -- quoting the reader's list
  "makes this a correction of the first rather than a second sample" -- and §13.100.2 measured what a second
  sample is worth (24 of 121 answers move). 20.0% against 20.8% says this pass delivers the second sample's rate
  and charges a call for it.
- **"Zero sold" is structural and therefore not evidence.** A decline is scored wrong on every capability whose
  gold is not a decline, so answering it can only buy or leave it; §13.128.2's one-sided property is confirmed by
  construction, not by this table. The roster-wide declined set does show 5 bought and 0 sold, which is the same
  fact.
- **The 4-of-10 bar was above the mechanism's own rate.** It is not that the dispatch was underpowered; it is
  that the registered bar (40%) is twice the rate the population converts at (20%), and that rate is the
  reader's.

The limitation is stated rather than papered over: the base rate is another 24 questions on the same route in the
same pairing, not the same ten questions on another draw. §13.149.6 states the instrument that would close it.

### 13.149.4 The four registered claims, read

| #   | claim (§13.141.5, route-corrected from §13.128.3)                             | measured                              | verdict       |
| --- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------- | ------------- |
| 1   | at least 4 of the 10 reachable questions convert to correct                   | **2**                                 | **falsified** |
| 2   | ABS does not move (29/30 question for question)                               | 0 bought, 0 sold of 30                | **holds**     |
| 3   | no question that did not decline changes verdict beyond the 5.0% reader floor | 24 of 448 = 5.36%, floor 22.4 +/- 9.2 | **holds**     |
| 4   | the counting questions are the ones most likely to convert                    | **0 of 4 counting, 2 of 6 not**       | **falsified** |

Claim 3 needs its arithmetic stated, because a 5.36% against a 5.0% floor looks like a failure and is not: the
floor is an **estimate** from 379 questions (§13.127.2), so the comparison carries its spread. 22.4 expected
flips with a standard deviation of 4.6 puts 24 inside one third of a standard deviation of the floor -- the
reader's own noise, not the treatment's.

Claim 4's falsifier was written before the run -- "zero of them convert while non-counting ones do" -- and that
is exactly what happened. It is the sharpest of the four: the corrective prompt carries an extra paragraph for
counting questions, and the four counting questions in the population converted **none**, while two of the six
non-counting ones did. §13.128.3 expected the opposite and explained why (the list averages 1.6 items against a
gold count of 3 to 10, so counting the list produces a specific wrong number rather than a recovery). That
explanation survives its own test; the prediction it supported does not.

### 13.149.5 Three numbers and one narrative this campaign published and then corrected

§13.148.4 first reported this census as "the population is half the size it was registered against" and "the
conversions are an order of magnitude below the claim", and both sentences were wrong. The record of what was
wrong is worth more than the correction, because the error was a **stale quote** rather than a misreading:

| what it said                                                                                                                   | what was true                     | why                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| registered 13-17 per run                                                                                                       | **10** per run                    | 13-17 is the module docstring's three-run figure across MR, TR **and** KU -- a capability census. §13.141.2 removed the six questions on routes the pass is not wired into and registered 10                                                                                       |
| "at least 5 of the 16"                                                                                                         | "at least **4 of the 10**"        | §13.141.5 restated the claim on the corrected population, and §13.147.1 was amended in the same dispatch                                                                                                                                                                           |
| "the 5 counting questions"                                                                                                     | **4**                             | five is the sixteen's count; four are on the reachable ten                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| "the bare ladder fires before the recovery pass can see the same question ... claimed in different orders on different routes" | the two passes **cannot** compete | §13.141.1 is a route table: the ladder is wired into `flat`/`temporal`/`assistant`/`knowledge-update` and explicitly not `multi-session`; the recovery pass is wired into `multi-session` only. §13.141.4 criterion 7 asserts the disjointness by counting calls across two routes |

The fourth is the one that matters, because it was not a stale number but a **new narrative** that contradicted a
section two documents earlier that carries a passing test. 95 bare retries in the treatment against 92 in the
control is not evidence of two mechanisms competing for a question; it is evidence that §13.141.3's union repair
held, since the pre-repair derivation would have withdrawn all 92.

**The rule: a section that quotes a number quotes the section that derived it, and names the derivation's
correction when there is one.** §13.147.1 cited §13.141 for 13-17; §13.141.2 had already replaced it with 10 in
the same section the citation pointed at. Both numbers were in the document, and the quotation kept the older
one.

### 13.149.6 What would make this decidable, and why it is not worth buying

The registered design is a sieve and its arithmetic is sound. At the base rate of 0.208 per question, a
population of 10 converts 2.08 per repetition; the bar is 4, so a single repetition clears it by chance
`P = 0.158`. Pooled over the four repetitions the arm already runs, `lambda = 8.3` and the bar is 16, which
chance clears with `P = 0.011`. **A sieve at 1% false positive is a good sieve.**

What it has no power against is the mechanism it is aimed at: at the measured rate the pooled expectation is
8.3, so the probability of clearing 16 is indistinguishable from zero. The population would have to convert at
**192% of its own base rate** for this design to read a pass. No re-ask mechanism was ever going to do that, and
the number that says so is 2.08.

So the design worth building is not a bigger sieve, it is a **paired counterfactual on the population itself**:

- **Within one treatment artifact**, identify the questions consulted in repetition _k_ (`recoveryAttempted`,
  §13.146) and read their outcomes in the repetitions where the pass did **not** consult them -- the same
  questions, the same route, the same reader, the same dispatch, with and without the mechanism. That is the only
  counterfactual in this campaign that does not lean on another capability's rate or another dispatch's drift.
- **The grid is what makes it readable** (`cedc847`), and the reach marks are what make the population
  identifiable per repetition (`4f013cb`). Both shipped after this pair was dispatched, which is why this section
  is one pairing of sixteen possible ones.
- **The bar would be the population's own unconsulted rate**, not a number chosen in advance: if the pass
  converts 2 of 10 while those same ten convert 0 of 10 in an untreated repetition, that is a mechanism; if they
  convert 2 of 10 either way, it is a re-roll.

**This is registered as the design, and not as the next dispatch.** The prior from §13.149.3 is that it would
read the base rate, and a dispatch whose expected information is one already-measured rate is the measurement
§13.148.6 refuses to build. `recover` closes here: not because it is unmeasurable, but because it has been
measured, and what it does to its population is what the reader does on its own.

### 13.149.7 The tool, and its acceptance criteria

`tools/recovery-reach.mjs`, invoked as

```
node tools/recovery-reach.mjs --control <report.json> --treatment <report.json> [--json]
```

| #   | criterion                                                            | test (`tools/__tests__/test_recovery_reach.py`)                                                                                                     |
| --- | -------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 1   | the population is the product's predicate, not a copy of it          | `test_counts_a_listed_decline_and_not_the_shapes_that_only_look_like_one` -- an absence-opener bullet and a bare decline are both excluded          |
| 2   | the reach is a route, not a capability name                          | `test_the_population_is_the_route_and_not_the_capability_name` -- an identical listed decline on `TR` is not in the population but is in the census |
| 3   | the population is read from the control                              | `test_the_population_comes_from_the_control_because_the_treatment_overwrote_the_reply` -- 2, not 0, when the treatment overwrote both replies       |
| 4   | a net never stands in for a flow                                     | `test_a_purchase_and_a_loss_are_both_named_because_a_net_hides_a_cancellation`                                                                      |
| 5   | the route the pass cannot reach is split out                         | `test_the_route_it_cannot_reach_is_split_out_from_every_other_capability`                                                                           |
| 6   | claim 1 is a floor of four, and the boundary is inclusive            | `..._falsified_when_the_pass_converts_fewer_than_four`, `..._holds_at_four`                                                                         |
| 7   | claim 3 is compared against the floor's spread, not its point value  | `test_a_flow_inside_the_readers_own_spread_is_not_called_a_falsification`                                                                           |
| 8   | claim 4 is falsified by its own stated falsifier                     | `test_the_counting_claim_is_falsified_by_its_own_stated_falsifier`                                                                                  |
| 9   | the same file twice is refused                                       | `test_refuses_the_same_file_twice`                                                                                                                  |
| 10  | an unpaired population question is refused                           | `test_refuses_a_population_question_the_treatment_does_not_carry`                                                                                   |
| 11  | an absent `answer` is not a decline                                  | `test_refuses_an_absent_answer_field_because_absent_is_not_a_decline`                                                                               |
| 12  | a non-boolean verdict is refused                                     | `test_refuses_a_verdict_that_is_not_a_boolean`                                                                                                      |
| 13  | an empty population is a wrong control                               | `test_refuses_a_control_with_no_reachable_population`                                                                                               |
| 14  | `attempted: 0` against a non-empty population is an assembly failure | `test_a_treatment_that_consulted_nothing_is_an_assembly_failure_not_a_reading` -- exit 1, not 2                                                     |
| 15  | the machine and human readings carry the same population             | `test_json_mode_carries_the_same_numbers_as_the_text`                                                                                               |

Mutation, stated so a later refactor cannot silently pass: replacing `declinedItems` with a local copy of the
bullet regex fails criterion 1 (the absence-opener); reading the population from the treatment fails criterion 3;
replacing the gross flow with a net fails criterion 4; comparing claim 3 to `5.0%` as a point value fails
criterion 7 on the flow `5.05%` in the fixture.

### 13.149.8 The rule this adds

**A treatment that can only fire on questions already scored wrong has a countable numerator and no denominator,
so its population's own conversion rate is the reading and the roster mean is not.** The corollary is the one
this campaign needed earlier: for such a treatment, **the counterfactual is the same questions without the
treatment**, and any comparison against `0` is comparing against a number the reader does not obey.

## 13.150 The retrieval ceiling is 44 questions, not five: §13.126 measured permutations and called it retrieval

§13.126 priced the retrieval axis at five questions and used that number to retire three registered increments and
to warn off a fourth. The arithmetic in it is correct and the question it answers is not the question the plan
needed answered. This section prices the other one, offline, from the artifact that was already on disk.

The ceiling of a mechanism that changes **which region** of the pool is delivered is **44 of 83 wrong questions,
8.80 points of the roster.** The ceiling of a mechanism that changes the **order** of what was delivered is 5. The
two are not the same number and they were not the same mechanism, and §13.126 read the second as a statement about
both.

### 13.150.1 Why the two counts came apart

`goldRanks` is a list with one entry per eligible gold turn. `carried` is how many of those turns reached the
reader. §13.126's count is the questions whose **best** rank is at ten or beyond -- and "best" is the operative
word:

| question                                              | golds | carried | best rank | §13.126                       | this section               |
| ----------------------------------------------------- | ----: | ------: | --------: | ----------------------------- | -------------------------- |
| `0a995998` (MR, wrong)                                |    17 |      17 |         8 | the reader had what it needed | nothing left to deliver    |
| a hypothetical with 17 golds, 12 carried, best rank 8 |    17 |      12 |         8 | the reader had what it needed | **five golds undelivered** |

The first row is real and the second is why the count cannot be read as retrieval. A question can have its first
gold near the top and five others the delivery dropped, and no permutation of a list produces a turn the list does
not contain. §13.126.1 says as much in one sentence -- "no permutation of a list improves the position of an element
that is already first" -- and then applies the count to mechanisms that are not permutations.

### 13.150.2 The ledger, over the control's 83 wrong questions

`tools/expand-resolution.mjs --artifact 40751394094`:

| capability |  wrong | carried = total | missing gold | of the missing: deep in pool | outside pool | region ceiling | in points |
| ---------- | -----: | --------------: | -----------: | ---------------------------: | -----------: | -------------: | --------: |
| IE         |     10 |               5 |            5 |                           16 |            2 |              5 |      3.33 |
| **MR**     | **34** |          **20** |       **14** |                        **0** |       **25** |         **14** | **11.57** |
| KU         |     11 |               0 |           11 |                           51 |           10 |             11 |     15.28 |
| **TR**     | **27** |          **14** |       **13** |                        **0** |       **21** |         **13** | **10.24** |
| ABS        |      1 |               0 |            1 |                            5 |            0 |              1 |      3.33 |
| **roster** | **83** |          **39** |       **44** |                       **72** |       **58** |         **44** |  **8.80** |

Three readings, and the third is the one that changes what the plan does next.

**1. Thirty-nine wrong questions are beyond every retrieval mechanism, and that number is now measured rather
than assumed.** They delivered every eligible gold they had. Whatever is wrong with them is in what the reader did
with the text, which is where §13.123's and §13.124's populations live. §13.126 reached the same conclusion from
the other side -- "the reading side owns the 78" -- and this table says 39 of them own it outright.

**2. The cheap bucket and the expensive bucket are disjoint by capability.** MR and TR have **zero** golds that the
index surfaced and the delivery dropped: every one of their 46 missing golds is outside the pool. KU is the
opposite: 51 of its 61 missing golds were surfaced and not delivered, and 51 is the largest single bucket in the
table. So "deliver more of what the index found" is a KU-and-IE mechanism and "search differently" is an MR-and-TR
mechanism, and a dispatch that does one will move the other's column by nothing.

**3. KU's 51 is a budget finding wearing a retrieval costume.** Those golds are in the pool; promoting them costs
characters and no retrieval at all. §13.139 measured the room: 468 of 500 questions render at or above 95% of the
48,000 ceiling and the tightest has 409 characters left. So the cheapest single bucket in the table is the one the
budget forbids, which is §13.147's "the denominator is the binding constraint" arriving on the retrieval axis.

### 13.150.3 The independent cross-check against the reference pipeline

§13.137.2 records the reference's single-variable pair: same day, same levers, one flag removed. MR **85.0 → 82.0**
with the reranker, so roughly **3.6 MR questions**. That is the _permutation_ axis and it lands under §13.126's
ceiling of 2 MR questions -- the two derivations agreeing on a small number is why §13.126's arithmetic is trusted.

The `--expand` movement is a different pair and it lands on the _region_ axis: MR **75.9 → 85.0 = +9.1 points =
11.0 questions**, TR **85.7 → 94.0 = +8.3 points = 10.5 questions**. Against this section's ceilings of **14** and
**13**, both numbers fit underneath, and they fit with room rather than filling it:

| axis | mechanism              | this roster's ceiling | the reference's measured movement |                                                          ratio |
| ---- | ---------------------- | --------------------: | --------------------------------: | -------------------------------------------------------------: |
| MR   | permutation (reranker) |                     2 |                               3.6 | 1.8x -- over, which is why the two runs disagree by a question |
| MR   | region (`--expand`)    |                **14** |                          **11.0** |                                                           0.79 |
| TR   | region (`--expand`)    |                **13** |                          **10.5** |                                                           0.81 |

The region rows are the useful ones. A mechanism claiming to move 11 or 10.5 questions on this roster would be
making a claim its own ledger permits, and a mechanism claiming 20 would not. That is what a ceiling is for: it does
not say a mechanism works, it says whether its claim is arithmetically possible.

It also says the two published `--expand` movements are **consistent with a per-question count**, which is the
first time this campaign has had a second derivation of that number from a source that did not know it was
computing one.

> **The third source below was read wrong, and §13.151 corrects it.** The paper's +7-11% is the effect of its
> `time-aware query expansion`, and that mechanism — read from the authors' code — is a **permutation**: an LLM
> infers a date range and the sessions inside it are moved to the front of an already-retrieved list. It is not a
> region change, so it does not belong on this axis, and citing it here as support for a per-entity retrieval was
> the same class of error §13.126 made in the other direction. The table is kept with its correction rather than
> deleted, because the coincidence it describes is real and the reason it is a coincidence is the finding.

**And there is a third source, which is what makes the interval an interval rather than a coincidence.**
LongMemEval's own paper (arXiv 2410.10813) reports time-aware query expansion at **+7-11% on temporal reasoning**.
On this roster that is **8.9-14.0 TR questions**, and the ceiling above is 13:

| source                               |   what it prices on TR | method                                                   | what it does not know                                   |
| ------------------------------------ | ---------------------: | -------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- |
| the paper's ablation                 | **8.9-14.0 questions** | one mechanism, one benchmark, the authors' own harness   | reported on the temporal category only                  |
| this section's ceiling               |       **13 questions** | arithmetic over the control's gold ledger, no model call | an upper bound, silent on whether a rule set reaches it |
| the reference's single-variable pair |     **10.5 questions** | one flag removed, same day, same levers                  | it mixes three cue classes into one switch              |

Three derivations and three methods -- another group's ablation, a published artifact's ledger, and a
reimplementation's paired run -- and the reference's measured movement sits inside both of the other two. That is
the strongest form this campaign has for a number it has not dispatched: bounded from above by its own arithmetic,
bracketed from outside by an independent ablation, matched in the middle by a build of the mechanism it is about to
register.

The same table explains why §13.126's five was never going to agree with any of them. The paper reports a
**recall** movement at +7-11%; §13.126 counts questions whose **best** gold is already past rank ten. Both
sentences can be true, and only one of them can price a time-aware query expansion.

### 13.150.4 The first rule set measured the wrong cue, and the roster's own wording says so

§13.137.3 describes `--expand` as "rules, not a model call": it parses time cues, counting cues and comparison cues
and issues one retrieval per named thing. The first version of this tool implemented three families -- an **absolute
named period**, a cardinality word, a conjunction -- and reported that a question could be split 9 times out of the
44 reachable ones. That number was a measurement of the rule set and not of the mechanism, and reading the
questions is what showed it:

| cue family                                                                                | wrong questions it matches (of 83) |     share |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------: | --------: |
| cardinality (`how many`, `total`)                                                         |                                 34 |     41.0% |
| conjunction (`and`, `or`, `vs`)                                                           |                                 20 |     24.1% |
| **relative period** (`last month`, `past three months`, `two weeks ago`, `most recently`) |                             **16** | **19.3%** |
| ordering (`what is the order`, `earliest`, `which came first`)                            |                                 10 |     12.0% |
| magnitude (`percentage`, `discount`, `how old`)                                           |                                  8 |      9.6% |
| **absolute period** (`in March`, `on Tuesdays`, a year)                                   |                              **5** |  **6.0%** |

**The family the first version had, the absolute period, is the rarest one on this roster at 6.0%.** The questions
say `How many plants did I acquire in the last month?`, `What is the total amount of money I earned from selling my
products at the markets?`, `What was the significant business milestone I mentioned four weeks ago?` -- they name a
period **relative to now**, and a rule that looks for month names finds almost none of them. §13.137.3's own
description ("`analyzeQuery` resolves a named period against `now`") already said the resolution was against `now`;
the first implementation read the first half of that clause and dropped the second.

Rebuilt as six families -- adding relative period, ordering and magnitude -- the same roster reads:

| capability | wrong | decomposable |  share | reachable **and** decomposable |
| ---------- | ----: | -----------: | -----: | -----------------------------: |
| IE         |    10 |            3 |  30.0% |                              1 |
| MR         |    34 |           18 |  52.9% |                          **7** |
| KU         |    11 |            3 |  27.3% |                              3 |
| TR         |    27 |           10 |  37.0% |                              5 |
| ABS        |     1 |            1 | 100.0% |                              1 |
| roster     |    83 |           35 |  42.2% |                         **17** |

**17 of 44, up from 9.** And with that, the arithmetic against the reference stops being a contradiction: a rule set
this size reaches 7 of MR's 14, and the reference moved 11 -- still more than the rules can address and no longer
twice as much.

### 13.150.5 The holdout that keeps a hand-written rule set honest

The six families were read off the **wrong** questions' own text, so their coverage of those questions is a fitted
quantity. Citing it as evidence that the rules work would be the §13.137 error in a new place -- a number that looks
like a finding and is a description of how it was chosen. The tool therefore reports the same families against the
questions the arm got **right**, on text they were not chosen against:

| capability | wrong, split |     share | correct, split |     share |       delta |
| ---------- | -----------: | --------: | -------------: | --------: | ----------: |
| IE         |         3/10 |     30.0% |         37/140 |     26.4% |        +3.6 |
| MR         |        18/34 |     52.9% |          48/87 |     55.2% |    **-2.2** |
| KU         |         3/11 |     27.3% |          11/61 |     18.0% |        +9.2 |
| **TR**     |    **10/27** | **37.0%** |     **78/100** | **78.0%** |   **-41.0** |
| ABS        |          1/1 |    100.0% |           9/29 |     31.0% | +69.0 (n=1) |
| roster     |        35/83 |     42.2% |        183/417 |     43.9% |        -1.7 |

**The roster-level delta is -1.7 points, which is the answer that matters: the rules generalise.** 42.2% against
43.9% on 500 questions is not a rule set fitted to the 83 failures; it is a description of how this dataset writes
questions. IE, MR and KU all sit within a few points of their holdout, and ABS's +69.0 is one question and is
reported for completeness rather than read.

**TR's -41.0 is the exception, and it is the most useful number in the table.** 78% of the temporal questions the
arm answers _correctly_ are splittable, and only 37% of the ones it gets wrong are. The ordering questions --
`What is the order of the six museums I visited from earliest to latest?` -- are the splittable ones and the arm
already answers them. What it fails on is the other shape: `What gardening-related activity did I do two weeks
ago?`, `What was the life event of one of my relatives that I participated in a week ago?` -- a **single** event at
a **relative** offset, where the key is not a decomposition at all but `now - 2 weeks` resolved into a window.

So TR's ceiling of 13 and MR's ceiling of 14 are close numbers produced by **different mechanisms**, and a rule set
that raises MR's coverage does nothing for TR's:

|     | what the failures need                                      | does a per-entity decomposition help                                   |
| --- | ----------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| MR  | an item that spans sessions and has no name in the question | partly -- the period narrows it, the items still have to be enumerated |
| TR  | one event at a relative offset                              | **no** -- it needs `now` arithmetic and a windowed retrieval           |
| KU  | a fact that changed, whose current value is the answer      | no -- it needs a recency or supersession rule                          |

**That is why this section does not register a dispatch.** The three columns want three mechanisms, and the only
one of them a rule set addresses is MR's, partially. Registering "`expand`" as one increment would put all three
under one switch and one number, which is the §13.125 portfolio problem and the §13.137.2 multi-variable problem
arriving together.

### 13.150.6 What the next action is, and why it is a source read rather than a run

The rule set **is** the mechanism. §13.137.5's rule -- a number in a comparison table must be recomputable from the
other side's artifacts -- has an obvious extension: a _mechanism_ compared against must be readable as code before a
reimplementation of it is registered. Three specific things are needed from that read, and each is a number this
section cannot produce:

1. **The cue list itself.** Six families reach 17 of 44; whether the reference's list reaches more is a question
   about its source, and 11 of 14 on MR is currently explained only by "its rules are richer than mine".
2. **What it does with the resolved period.** "One retrieval per named thing" says nothing about whether a
   relative period is converted into a filter over turn timestamps, a boost, or a separate index.
3. **Whether the expansion runs before or after the top-k cut**, because that is the difference between the cheap
   bucket (72 golds the index found and the delivery dropped) and the expensive one (58 it never found), and this
   roster's two buckets are disjoint by capability.

Until then the honest statement is the one the ledger supports: **the region ceiling is 44 questions and 8.80
points, a hand-written six-family rule set reaches 17 of them, and the reference's measured MR movement of 11 sits
between the two.**

### 13.150.7 What §13.126 said next, restated

§13.126.4 wrote: "a retrieval mechanism must name its ceiling before it is dispatched, and the ceiling is computed
from the same five columns above." The four columns were wrong for the class of mechanism the paragraph was
warning off, and the reason is one word in the criterion:

> the count of wrong questions in its target capability whose best gold rank is at or beyond the cut it operates on

"best gold rank" is a permutation quantity. A mechanism that adds a delivery is not bounded by it, and a mechanism
that adds a delivery is what the reference runs for MR and TR. The corrected criterion, which is what
`tools/expand-resolution.mjs` computes:

- **A permutation mechanism** names its ceiling as wrong questions whose **best** gold is at or beyond its cut.
- **A region mechanism** names its ceiling as wrong questions with **at least one** eligible gold outside the
  delivery, split into the part the index already found (cheap) and the part it never found (expensive).
- **A mechanism that does neither** -- one that changes the instruction, the rendering or the reader -- has a
  ceiling of the wrong questions it can address at all, and §13.126's count is not it either.

### 13.150.8 The tool, and its acceptance criteria

```
node tools/expand-resolution.mjs --artifact <report.json> [--json]
```

| #   | criterion                                                                           | test (`tools/__tests__/test_expand_resolution.py`)                                  |
| --- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 1   | a question whose golds were all delivered is not in the ceiling                     | `test_a_question_whose_golds_were_all_delivered_is_not_reachable`                   |
| 2   | a gold the index saw and the delivery dropped is the cheap bucket                   | `test_a_gold_the_index_saw_and_the_delivery_dropped_is_the_cheap_bucket`            |
| 3   | a gold the index never surfaced is the expensive bucket                             | `test_a_gold_the_index_never_surfaced_is_the_expensive_bucket`                      |
| 4   | a delivery wider than the pool is read at its tight side, not as a negative         | `test_a_delivery_wider_than_the_pool_is_read_at_its_tight_side`                     |
| 5   | a record written before `poolGold` keeps its missing count and loses only the split | `test_a_record_without_a_pool_is_still_priced_for_its_missing_golds`                |
| 6   | a correct question never enters a ceiling                                           | `test_a_correct_question_never_enters_the_ceiling`                                  |
| 7   | the two ceilings are two numbers, and region dominates permutation                  | `test_the_two_ceilings_are_two_numbers_and_the_region_one_dominates`                |
| 8   | all-negative ranks are a region target and not a permutation one                    | `test_a_question_with_no_gold_in_the_pool_is_not_a_permutation_target`              |
| 9   | the ceiling is also reported in points                                              | `test_the_ceiling_is_reported_in_points_because_that_is_the_unit_it_is_compared_in` |
| 10  | a question with no cue is one sub-query                                             | `test_a_question_with_no_cue_is_one_sub_query`                                      |
| 11  | a named period is a temporal cue                                                    | `test_a_named_period_is_a_temporal_cue`                                             |
| 12  | a conjunction names two things at once                                              | `test_a_conjunction_names_two_things_at_once`                                       |
| 13  | the decomposable count is over wrong questions and the reach is a subset            | `test_the_decomposable_count_is_over_wrong_questions_and_the_reach_is_a_subset`     |
| 14  | `carried` above `total` is refused                                                  | `test_refuses_a_delivery_that_exceeds_its_own_denominator`                          |
| 15  | a pool larger than the set it is a subset of is refused                             | `test_refuses_a_pool_larger_than_its_denominator`                                   |
| 16  | a `goldRanks` list of the wrong length is refused                                   | `test_refuses_a_rank_list_that_does_not_match_its_denominator`                      |
| 17  | a non-boolean verdict is refused                                                    | `test_refuses_a_verdict_that_is_not_a_boolean`                                      |
| 18  | a report with no roster is refused                                                  | `test_refuses_a_report_with_no_roster`                                              |
| 19  | an absent overlap is unjudgeable, not complete                                      | `test_an_absent_overlap_is_unjudgeable_rather_than_complete`                        |
| 20  | an unknown flag is a usage error                                                    | `test_an_unknown_flag_is_a_usage_error_not_a_reading`                               |
| 21  | the text and machine readings agree                                                 | `test_the_text_reading_carries_the_same_population_as_the_machine_one`              |
| 22  | the holdout counts the questions the rules were not chosen against                  | `test_the_holdout_counts_the_questions_the_rules_were_not_chosen_against`           |
| 23  | a relative period is a cue, and it is not the same key as an absolute one           | `test_a_relative_period_is_a_cue_because_the_roster_says_so`                        |
| 24  | an ordering question is a different key from a cardinality one                      | `test_an_ordering_question_is_a_different_key_from_a_cardinality_one`               |
| 25  | the holdout is printed, not only stored                                             | `test_the_text_reading_prints_the_holdout`                                          |

Mutation, stated so a later refactor cannot silently pass: reading `carried` as `total - missing` fails criterion
1; treating an absent `pool` as zero fails criterion 5 (every missing gold becomes outside-pool); a
`Math.max(0, pool - carried)` dropped in favour of the identity fails criterion 4 with a negative; computing the
permutation ceiling from `max` instead of `min` fails criterion 7 on the `hidden` fixture; dropping the
`relative-period` family fails criterion 23 and takes the roster's decomposable count from 35 to 24; counting a
conjunction as one key instead of two fails criterion 12 (the fixture expects three).

### 13.150.9 The rule this adds

**A ceiling is priced in the unit of the mechanism, and "retrieval" is at least two mechanisms.** A count computed
from the best rank bounds permutations; a count computed from delivered versus eligible bounds region changes; and
the second is 8.8 times the first on this roster. Applying the smaller one to the larger class does not make the
larger class unreachable -- it makes the plan stop looking, which is the same outcome with worse bookkeeping.

And the corollary this section paid for twice: **a hand-written rule set is a measurement of the corpus's wording,
so it has to be read back against that wording before its coverage is quoted.** The first six-line version of the
cue table had an absolute-period family that matched 6.0% of the failures, while the relative form matched 19.3%;
the coverage it reported was a fact about the rule, dressed as a fact about the mechanism. The holdout is what makes
the difference visible: 42.2% of the wrong questions and 43.9% of the right ones means the rules describe the
dataset, and TR's 37.0% against 78.0% means one capability's failures need a different mechanism rather than a
better rule.

## 13.151 The reference's time-aware expansion is a permutation, and reading its code is what said so

§13.137.3 described the retrieval-side lever as "**rules, not a model call**": `analyzeQuery` parses cues and
issues one retrieval per named thing, costing a handful of vector searches and no extra LLM call. That
description is of `al-buddy-memory`'s `--expand` flag, which is one implementation. LongMemEval's **own**
implementation is a different mechanism, it is public (`src/index_expansion/temp_query_search_pruning.py` in
`xiaowu0162/LongMemEval`), and reading it settles three questions this campaign has been guessing at since
§13.137.
